items.title: What it does
items.text:
• Automatic grid detection

    Regular (ERA5, CMIP), curvilinear and rotated-pole (NEMO, CORDEX, WRF) and unstructured (ICON) grids are recognised from the dataset itself.

  • Conservative remapping

    Conservative and nearest-neighbour remapping with ESMF weights, on the sphere or the WGS84 ellipsoid.

  • A shared weights store

    Weights are computed once per source grid, HEALPix level and method, and reused by everyone pointing at the same directory.

  • Point binning

    Swaths, stations and trajectories, where every sample has its own position, are binned into HEALPix cells.

  • Pyramids

    From the finest level down to level 0, with mean or mode coarsening and valid fractions for masked fields.

  • Parallel writes

    Zarr stores in one call, or split into independent tasks for HPC array jobs.

  • Region selection

    By bounding box, cone or cell list, also for stores without coordinate arrays.

  • CF metadata

    The CF healpix grid mapping and a record of how every level was built.

Regridding and coarsening run lazily on dask arrays.

items.title: Quick example
items.text:
import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

ds = xr.open_mfdataset("data/*.nc")
pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid()  # finest level from the grid resolution
gd.save_pyramid(pyramid, "/path/to/output", mode="w")

create_healpix_pyramid computes the remapping weights on the first run and takes them from the weights store afterwards.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
grid-doctor is installed from GitHub:

python -m pip install git+https://github.com/freva-org/grid-doctor.git

For GPU-accelerated weight application, add the gpu extra, which installs CuPy:

python -m pip install "grid-doctor[gpu] @ git+https://github.com/freva-org/grid-doctor.git"

items.title: ESMF
items.text:
Remapping weights are generated with ESMF: in memory through its Python bindings (ESMPy), or for large grids with the parallel ESMF_RegridWeightGen command under MPI. ESMF is not available from PyPI; install it from conda-forge:

mamba install -c conda-forge "esmf=*=mpi_openmpi_*" esmpy

On an HPC system, pick the MPI build that matches the system's MPI library. ESMF is only needed to generate weights. Applying existing weight files, binning point data, coarsening, selecting regions and writing stores work without it.

items.title: Your first pyramid
items.text:
import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

ds = xr.open_mfdataset("path/to/*.nc")
pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid()
gd.save_pyramid(pyramid, "/path/to/output", mode="w")

The finest level follows from the resolution of the source grid; pass max_level= to choose it yourself. save_pyramid writes one Zarr store per level, level_0.zarr, level_1.zarr, …, below /path/to/output. The weights are computed on the first run and reused from the weights store on every later run with the same grid. Set GRID_DOCTOR_WEIGHTS_STORE to share them with others, see Configuration.

items.title: Writing to S3
items.text:
Pass an s3:// URL and the storage options. get_s3_options reads the access and secret key from a JSON file with the fields accessKey and secretKey:

gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    "s3://my-bucket/my-dataset",
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options("https://s3.example.org", "~/.s3-credentials.json"),
)

Keep credentials out of scripts

Read secrets from a credentials file or the environment, and never commit them to a repository.

items.title: Conversion scripts
items.text:
grid_doctor.cli.get_parser returns an argument parser with the options --s3-bucket, --s3-endpoint, --s3-credentials-file and -v already defined:

import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd
import grid_doctor.cli as gd_cli

parser = gd_cli.get_parser("my-dataset", "Convert my-dataset to HEALPix.")
parser.add_argument("files", nargs="+")
args = parser.parse_args()
gd_cli.setup_logging_from_args(args)

ds = xr.open_mfdataset(args.files)
pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid()
gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    f"s3://{args.s3_bucket}/my-dataset",
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options(args.s3_endpoint, args.s3_credentials_file),
)

python convert.py --s3-bucket my-bucket --s3-endpoint https://s3.example.org data/*.nc -vv

items.title: Logging
items.text:
Each -v on the command line raises the log level:

Flags Level (none) WARNING -v INFO -vv DEBUG

Outside a script, set the level directly:

import grid_doctor as gd

gd.setup_logging(level="DEBUG")  # or verbosity=2

items.title: Working with the data
items.text: A HEALPix pyramid written by grid-doctor is a set of ordinary Zarr stores, one per level. Global levels up to the coordinate threshold (level 10 by default) carry latitude/longitude arrays and work with any xarray or HEALPix-aware tool. This page covers what is different about the rest: regions, very high levels and stores without coordinate arrays.

items.title: Opening a level
items.text:
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_zarr(
    "s3://my-bucket/my-dataset/level_9.zarr",
    storage_options={"anon": True, "endpoint_url": "https://s3.example.org"},
    chunks=None,
)

chunks=None gives plain lazy Zarr-backed arrays that are sliced in proportion to what you select. With the default dask chunking, xarray builds a description of the global chunk grid when opening: harmless at low levels, millions of entries at level 16 and nearly a billion at level 20, where opening hangs before any data moves. Open high levels with chunks=None and select a region before loading anything.

The cells are equal-area, so a global or domain mean is a plain mean over cells, with no latitude weighting:

ds["tas"].mean("cell")

Fields with missing values

For variables with missing values (ocean-only fields, observation gaps), cells on coarser levels can be only partly valid, and a plain mean over cells is biased. If the store has a <name>_valid_fraction variable, use it as the weight, see Coarsening and averaging masked fields:

ds.sst.weighted(ds.sst_valid_fraction.fillna(0)).mean("cell")

items.title: Selecting a region
items.text:
grid-doctor's select_bbox and select_cone read only the chunks a region touches and return a small, loaded dataset:

import grid_doctor as gd

berlin = ds.gd.select_bbox(lon=(13.1, 13.8), lat=(52.3, 52.7))
station = ds.gd.select_cone(lon=13.41, lat=52.52, radius=0.05)  # degrees

The result is a compact subset: its cell coordinate holds the global HEALPix indices, and latitude/longitude are computed for the selected cells. It covers the region, so cells straddling the edge are included; cut the exact box with the coordinates if you need to:

inside = (
    (berlin.longitude >= 13.1) & (berlin.longitude <= 13.8)
    & (berlin.latitude >= 52.3) & (berlin.latitude <= 52.7)
)
berlin = berlin.isel(cell=inside.values.nonzero()[0])

select_cells extracts a list of cell indices, for example the same cells from another dataset.

items.title: Stores without coordinate arrays
items.text:
At high levels a global coordinate array is useless: level 16 has about 5.2 × 10¹⁰ cells, and latitude/longitude would take hundreds of gigabytes while carrying no information, because HEALPix coordinates are a function of the cell index. Levels above the threshold are therefore written without them (save_pyramid(write_coords=...) controls this). Such stores carry only the crs grid mapping and the attribute grid_doctor_implicit_coords = 1.

Nothing changes for the selection functions: they compute the coordinates of exactly the cells they return. For cells you sliced yourself, attach_cell_coords adds them:

import numpy as np

part = ds.isel(cell=slice(start, stop))
part = part.gd.attach_cell_coords(np.arange(start, stop), level=16)

items.title: Comparing levels and datasets
items.text:
In nested ordering the parent of a cell is a bit shift away: the level-9 parent of a level-16 cell is cell >> 14, two bits per level. To put a high-resolution selection next to a coarser dataset, select the parents there, no interpolation needed:

parents = np.unique(berlin["cell"].values >> (2 * (16 - 9)))
era5_berlin = era5_level9.gd.select_cells(parents)

Datasets at the same level and with the same definition (sphere or ellipsoid, see the technical decisions) can be compared cell by cell directly.

items.title: Plotting
items.text:
The selection is a normal dataset with per-cell coordinates:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.scatter(berlin["longitude"], berlin["latitude"], c=berlin["t2m"], s=1)
plt.colorbar(label="t2m")

At high levels a scatter of cell centres looks like a raster at typical figure sizes. For a quick overview, open a coarse level of the same pyramid, which carries coordinates and works in any HEALPix viewer.

items.title: How the selection works
items.text: Every cell at a coarse level corresponds to one contiguous range of cells at a fine level: parent p at level L - Δ is the range [p · 4^Δ, (p + 1) · 4^Δ) at level L. The selection functions find the coarse cells that cover the region (at level - query_delta, eight levels coarser by default), merge neighbouring ranges, and read each as one slice. When the store is chunked at a power of four, each range is whole chunks: a city-sized box at level 16 is a handful of contiguous reads. Setting query_delta to the store's chunk exponent reads no data outside the covering cells.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Opening hangs or uses a lot of memory default dask chunking at a high level chunks=None MemoryError on .load() or .values loading the global cell dimension select a region first No latitude/longitude store without coordinate arrays use the selection functions or attach_cell_coords Slow reads for a small region query_delta not aligned with the store chunks set query_delta to the chunk exponent Fields shifted by up to ~14 km comparing sphere and ellipsoid data use data on the same definition

items.title: Technical decisions
items.text: This document records the design rationale behind the significant technical choices in grid-doctor1, the software that produces the HEALPix datasets: how data is remapped or binned to HEALPix, how pyramids are coarsened and what metadata the stores carry. It is intended as a reference for contributors, reviewers, and users of the HEALPix pyramids.

items.title: Why HEALPix?
items.text: HEALPix (Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelisation) tiles the sphere into pixels of exactly equal area at every resolution level. Originally developed for mapping the cosmic microwave background, it turns out to be exactly what analysis-ready climate data needs.

items.title: Area-weighted statistics are trivial
items.text:
Every pixel covers the same solid angle, so a global mean is just the arithmetic mean of all pixels. No latitude-dependent cosine weighting is needed, and an entire class of subtle statistics bugs, forgotten or misapplied area weights, simply cannot occur.

Fields with missing values

This holds for complete fields. For fields with NaNs (ocean-only variables, sea ice, observation gaps), a coarse cell can be partly valid, and its value is the mean over that valid part only. Averages over coarse levels then need the valid fraction of each cell as a weight;

Cells coloured by their relative area. On a lat-lon grid (left), cell areas shrink with latitude; on a comparable 0.25° grid the largest cell is more than 400 times bigger than the smallest. On HEALPix (right), every cell is identical by construction.

items.title: No singularities at the poles
items.text:
Regular lat-lon grids have converging meridians and vanishing cell areas at the poles, which force special-case handling in numerics, storage, and visualisation. HEALPix cells run right through the pole without anything special happening there.

Both grids viewed from directly above the North Pole (cross marks the pole). The lat-lon cells collapse into slivers at the centre; the HEALPix tessellation is unremarkable there, which is the point.

items.title: Nested ordering
items.text:
HEALPix defines two pixel numbering schemes: ring ordering (pixels numbered along iso-latitude rings) and nested ordering (pixels numbered by a hierarchical quad-tree). The remapping procedure1 defaults to nested ordering because it makes coarsening free.

In nested ordering, a parent pixel at level \(L\) with index \(i\) has children \(4i\), \(4i+1\), \(4i+2\), \(4i+3\) at level \(L+1\). Coarsening the full grid therefore reduces to reshaping the data array from \((n_\text{cells},)\) to \((n_\text{cells} / 4,\; 4)\) and reducing along the last axis, requiring no index lookup, no scatter, and no sorting.

A real level 2 cell (parent 11, amber) with its four level 3 children (44 to 47, teal) and sixteen level 4 grandchildren (thin outlines). The indices are the actual nested indices: children of parent p are 4p to 4p+3.

HEALPix also supports ring ordering, but it does not have contiguous parent-child layout. Our remapping software1 supports it, but in that mode every pyramid level is independently remapped from the source grid, which is substantially more expensive.

items.title: Sphere or ellipsoid
items.text:
HEALPix can be defined on a perfect sphere, the original construction2, or on the WGS84 ellipsoid7, where the cell boundaries are laid out in authalic latitude so that cells stay equal-area on the ellipsoid58. grid-doctor uses the sphere by default; set grid_doctor.config.ellipsoid = "WGS84" (or pass ellipsoid="WGS84") to remap and bin onto the ellipsoid instead. The output records the definition it uses.

Both definitions give the same results with ESMF, even though ESMF computes all overlap areas on the sphere6. healpix-geo returns the cell vertices of either definition in geodetic coordinates, the same coordinates the source data uses, so source and target mesh always share one coordinate space; the ellipsoidal definition only moves where the cell boundaries lie. The remaining distortion of the sphere approximation affects the numerator and denominator of every conservative weight3 almost equally and cancels to a relative error of about \(10^{-5}\) at level 10, smaller at finer levels.

What does not work is converting a remapped product from one definition to the other. Re-binning already averaged cells onto displaced cells adds a second interpolation step and roughly doubles the error. Products for either definition should always be remapped from the native data.

Route Product RMS error × local contrast A native → spherical HEALPix 0.0840 K 0.94 B native → ellipsoidal (WGS84) HEALPix 0.0841 K 0.94 C A converted to ellipsoidal 0.1639 K 1.84

One day of MODIS-Aqua night-time SST (4 km) remapped to HEALPix level 10 (about 6.4 km) with ESMF conservative weights, about 2.66 million ocean cells. Each route is scored against a reference that bins the native pixels directly into cells of the same definition. The local contrast (median spread within groups of four neighbouring cells, 0.089 K) is the relevant scale because remapping errors live at the cell scale. A and B agree within 1 % between 60° S and 45° N and within 5 % poleward of that.

items.title: Different definitions are different grids
items.text:
Two datasets on HEALPix at the same level are not on the same grid unless they use the same definition. The same cell index denotes a different patch of the Earth under the two definitions, displaced by the difference between geodetic and authalic latitude4:

\[ \varphi - \xi \approx \tfrac{e^2}{3} \sin 2\varphi \quad (\text{max } 7.7' \approx 14\ \mathrm{km\ at}\ 45°), \]

with WGS84 eccentricity \(e^2 \approx 0.006694\). That is about 2 cell widths at level 10, 9 at level 12 and 18 at level 13; at level 10, 99.8 % of all cells have a different index under the two definitions.

Data on different definitions must therefore not be compared, overlaid or differenced cell by cell, and cells must not be located with the other definition (for example lonlat_to_healpix with a different ellipsoid than the data was produced with). Otherwise the field appears shifted by up to 14 km: fronts, coastlines and swath edges land in the wrong cells. To compare such datasets, remap both from their native data onto the same definition.

items.title: Target level selection
items.text:
The target HEALPix level for each source dataset is chosen as the highest level whose characteristic pixel spacing is coarser than or comparable to the source resolution. The heuristic is:

\[ \ell = \left\lfloor \log_2 \frac{58.6°}{\Delta} \right\rfloor \]

where \(\Delta\) is the estimated source grid spacing in degrees. The constant 58.6° is the approximate pixel spacing at level 0, derived from \(360° \;/\; \sqrt{12 \times 4^0}\).

This ensures that the HEALPix grid does not oversample the source. Lower pyramid levels are derived by coarsening, not by remapping, so no additional information is fabricated.

Level nside Pixels Approx. spacing 0 1 12 58.6° 3 8 768 7.3° 5 32 12 288 1.8° 7 128 196 608 27.5′ 9 512 3 145 728 6.9′ 10 1024 12 582 912 3.4′

items.title: Remapping methods
items.text: Remapping is performed by ESMF, which computes the geometric overlap between source and target cells and produces a sparse weight matrix that is applied to the data. The remapping software supports two remapping methods, chosen by variable type.

items.title: Conservative remapping (continuous fields)
items.text:
Used for temperature, precipitation, radiation, wind, and all other fields that represent continuous physical quantities.

Conservative remapping computes area-weighted averages: each weight is proportional to the fractional overlap area between a source cell and a target cell. The key property is integral preservation, the area-integral of the field over any target cell equals the sum of the area-integrals of the contributing source cells.

This is the only method that correctly handles sub-pixel variability. If a HEALPix cell straddles a strong SST gradient, the conservative average reflects the true area-weighted mean rather than the value at a single sampled point.

items.title: Nearest-neighbour remapping (categorical fields)
items.text:
Used for land-sea masks, land cover classes, soil type, and all other fields where values are discrete labels.

Nearest-neighbour assigns each target cell the value of the closest source cell centre. This guarantees that the output contains only values that actually exist in the source, no interpolated intermediate classes like "land-use 3.7" can appear.

Linear or bilinear interpolation is explicitly not supported. While it can produce smoother-looking fields, it fabricates values that were not present in the original data.

items.title: Weight generation
items.text:
Remapping weights are precomputed and stored as reusable NetCDF files. Weight generation is the most expensive step in the pipeline, but it only needs to happen once per combination of source grid and target HEALPix level. Subsequent runs reuse the cached weight file.

For moderate grids, weights are generated in memory using ESMF's Python bindings (ESMPy). For very large grids where this would exceed available RAM, grid-doctor1 writes both meshes to temporary files and invokes the standalone ESMF_RegridWeightGen command under MPI, with a configurable number of ranks.

Grid-doctor1 automatically classifies the source grid and constructs the appropriate mesh representation:

Source type Examples Detection Regular ERA5, CMIP on lat-lon grids 1-D lat and lon coordinates Curvilinear NEMO, WRF 2-D lat(y, x) and lon(y, x) Unstructured ICON, MPAS Dimension named cell / ncells, or CDI_grid_type attribute

Every weight file is annotated with provenance metadata (grid_doctor_method, grid_doctor_level, grid_doctor_order, source grid details) so that downstream tools can verify how the weights were produced.

items.title: Weight application
items.text: Applying the weight matrix to data is a sparse matrix multiplication. The full batch of time steps is reshaped into a single dense matrix and multiplied in one operation, which is typically 10–50× faster than applying the weights one time step at a time. GPU acceleration (via CuPy) and JIT compilation (via Numba) are used automatically when those packages are installed. See Performance: application backends for details.

items.title: Missing-value handling during remapping
items.text: Source datasets commonly contain NaN values, for instance land pixels in an ocean dataset, gaps in satellite swaths, or masked regions. The missing_policy parameter controls how these are treated during weight application.

items.title: Renormalize (default)
items.text:
Source cells that are NaN are excluded from the weighted sum. The weights of the remaining valid source cells are rescaled so they sum to 1. A target cell receives a valid value as long as at least one contributing source cell is valid.

This is the appropriate choice for virtually all climate fields. A HEALPix cell on a coastline that partly overlaps land (NaN) and partly ocean still receives a valid SST from the ocean fraction.

items.title: Propagate
items.text:
If any contributing source cell is NaN, the target cell is set to NaN. No partial averages are computed.

This mode exists for strict budget-closure applications. If you are integrating total precipitation over a HEALPix cell and one source cell is missing, the renormalized average looks valid but represents a biased estimate over a subset of the area. For budget-closure studies it is preferable to have a NaN than a plausible-looking number derived from incomplete coverage.

Note that this mode is very aggressive: a single NaN source cell at the edge of a target cell's footprint is enough to discard it. Along coastlines, swath edges, and orbit gaps, large portions of the output will be NaN.

items.title: Point binning (swath and station data)
items.text:
Gridded datasets are remapped with ESMF as described above. Point-sampled data (satellite Level-2 swaths, station records, trajectories) cannot use that path for two structural reasons: every granule has unique geometry, so the precomputed weight matrix can never be reused, and ESMF's nearest source-to-destination method assigns a value to every destination cell, which would smear a narrow swath over the entire globe.

Point data is therefore binned: each sample is assigned to the HEALPix cell containing its coordinates and all samples per cell are reduced. The available reductions mirror the two remapping methods:

  • Mean binning (continuous fields). In the oversampled limit, with sample spacing much finer than the target cell spacing, the per-cell sample mean converges to the area-weighted mean, making it a first-order approximation of conservative remapping. This validity condition is enforced by choosing the target level from the sample spacing with the same heuristic used for gridded data; a swath is never binned into cells finer than its own pixel spacing.
  • Mode binning (categorical fields). The most frequent class per cell, the binning analogue of nearest-neighbour remapping. Ties are broken deterministically towards the lowest class value. As with nearest-neighbour remapping, no interpolated intermediate classes can appear.
  • min / max / count are available for extrema and coverage diagnostics.

A per-sample sum is deliberately not offered: it scales with sample density (orbit overlap, across-track pixel count) rather than any physical integral, and therefore violates the integral-preservation rationale that motivates conservative remapping. Root-mean-square reductions are likewise excluded because they do not commute with mean coarsening in the pyramid; if an RMS quantity is required, bin the squared field with the mean and apply the square root at read time.

items.title: Sphere or ellipsoid for satellite data
items.text: Satellite geolocation is geodetic (WGS84). Binning assigns each geodetic position to the cell that contains it, on the same definition as remapping: the sphere by default, the ellipsoid when configured. Binning on the sphere is as accurate as binning on the ellipsoid (see Sphere or ellipsoid). Data binned on one definition is not comparable cell by cell with data on the other: the cells are displaced by up to ~0.13° (~14 km) at 45° latitude, several to dozens of pixels at typical swath target levels.

items.title: Minimum sample count and coverage tracking
items.text: A cell is set to NaN when it receives fewer than min_count valid samples (default: 1). Optionally, a companion <variable>_count variable records the number of valid samples per cell. Publishing the count is recommended: it makes coverage auditable, enables unbiased count-weighted merging of overlapping granules, and is the point-data analogue of a valid-area fraction for coarsened grids.

items.title: Pyramids from binned data
items.text: Binned datasets carry the full standard metadata (crs grid mapping and grid_doctor_* attributes) and dense cell layout, so pyramid construction reuses the ordinary coarsening machinery unchanged, including the 50% minimum-valid-fraction rule. The recorded method (grid_doctor_method = "binned-mean" or "binned-mode") drives the automatic mean-vs-mode coarsening selection, just as "conservative" and "nearest" do for remapped data.

items.title: Pyramid construction and coarsening
items.text: The multi-resolution pyramid is built by first remapping the source dataset to the finest HEALPix level, then deriving all coarser levels by iterated coarsening, one level at a time, always a factor of 4. Every level builds on the previous one, so the whole pyramid is a single lazy computation (see Chunked application and single-pass writes).

items.title: Why coarsen rather than remap at each level?
items.text: Remapping from the original source grid at every level would be correct but wasteful: each level would require a separate weight file, and weight generation cost scales with the product of source and target cell counts. Coarsening is essentially free, a reshape plus a vectorised reduction, and produces identical results for nested HEALPix grids because the nested pixel hierarchy exactly matches the coarsening hierarchy.

items.title: Mean coarsening (continuous fields)
items.text:
For continuous fields (those remapped with conservative weights), each coarse cell's value is the mean over all valid finest-level cells beneath it. This is not the same as the mean of its 4 children once children are only partly valid: a child built from a single valid finest-level cell would otherwise count as much as a child built from four. Repeated over several levels, that mean of means drifts away from the finest level.

The pyramid therefore carries two running totals per cell instead of a mean: the sum of the valid finest-level values and their count. Both coarsen exactly by summing groups of 4, and the mean is only formed when a level is written:

\[ \bar{x}_\text{parent} = \frac{\sum_{c} s_c}{\sum_{c} n_c}, \qquad s_c = \sum_{\text{valid } i \in c} x_i, \quad n_c = \#\{\text{valid } i \in c\} \]

Every level is therefore identical to coarsening directly from the finest level, while each step stays a local reduction of 4 neighbouring cells. create_healpix_pyramid keeps these sums and counts internally while building its chain.

Be careful with manually chained mean coarsening

Chaining averages works for complete fields. With missing data, intermediate cells can represent different numbers of finest-level cells, but the next average weights them equally. Coarsen directly from finest, or use create_healpix_pyramid, instead.

items.title: Mode coarsening (categorical fields)
items.text:
For categorical fields (those remapped with nearest-neighbour weights), averaging class labels is meaningless. Instead, each parent cell receives the mode (most frequent value) of its valid children. Ties are broken by the first occurrence.

The coarsening mode is inferred automatically from the remapping method stored in the dataset attributes: grid_doctor_method = "nearest" triggers mode coarsening, "conservative" triggers mean coarsening. An explicit coarsen_mode parameter is available to override this.

Unlike the mean, a mode of modes is not the mode of all finest-level cells, and mode coarsening is applied level by level, with the minimum valid fraction checked against the 4 children at each step.

items.title: Minimum valid fraction (default: 50%)
items.text:
For mean coarsening, a cell is set to NaN when fewer than half of the finest-level cells beneath it are valid. The threshold is applied to this cumulative fraction, not to the 4 children of each step.

Representativeness. A cell's value should represent the majority of its area. Because the threshold uses the finest-level count, the value is guaranteed to cover at least half of the cell's area at every level. A per-step rule could not guarantee this: 2 valid children out of 4, each built from 2 valid children out of 4, cover only a quarter of the area two levels up. Below the threshold, a few pixels' values would "speak for" an area that has no data, which is indistinguishable from interpolation into unknown territory.

Cells masked by the threshold keep their running sums and counts, so their valid data still contributes to coarser levels where it is part of a majority.

Cascade prevention. Each coarsening step is a factor-of-4 reduction. If only 1 of 4 valid children were sufficient, a single valid pixel at the finest level could survive every coarsening step: 1/4 at level \(N-1\), that surviving parent is again 1/4 at level \(N-2\), and so on. After \(k\) steps it represents a fraction of \(4^{-k}\) of the area it claims to cover. This is the "Siberian lake problem" observed with MODIS SST: a single lake pixel at level 10 bled through 7 coarsening steps to level 3, covering a 16 384× larger area. With a 50% threshold, the cascade is impossible, the pixel is discarded at the very first step because 1/4 < 1/2. A feature can only survive coarsening if it covers at least half the area at every scale, which is exactly when it is a real, resolvable feature at that resolution.

The threshold is configurable with min_valid_fraction. Set it to 0 to keep every cell that contains any valid data, for instance when the coarse levels are only used for weighted aggregates.

items.title: Averaging over coarse levels: valid fractions
items.text:
Because every coarse value is a mean over its valid area, a plain mean over coarse cells weights a coastal cell that is 10% ocean as much as an open-ocean cell. The level-to-level consistency of the pyramid only holds for means weighted by the number of valid finest-level cells: with two coarse cells, one fully valid at 10 °C (4 valid cells) and one with a single valid cell at 20 °C, the finest-level mean is (4 × 10 + 20) / 5 = 12 °C, while the plain mean of the two coarse values is 15 °C. Both coarse values are correct; the plain average is not.

The weights cannot be folded into the stored values without losing their meaning (a coastal cell would no longer hold the SST of its ocean part). Instead, the pyramid can store them alongside:

pyramid = gd.create_healpix_pyramid(ds, valid_fraction=True)

adds <name>_valid_fraction (float32, fraction of valid finest-level cells, linked through the CF ancillary_variables attribute) to every level, including the finest one. Global or regional means then agree across all levels:

ds = pyramid[3]
ds.sst.weighted(ds.sst_valid_fraction.fillna(0)).mean("cell")

The option is opt-in because the fraction has the shape of its variable:

  • True stores a fraction for every cell variable, with its full shape. This is correct for masks that change over time or height (sea ice, clouds, orography on pressure levels).
  • "static" stores a single cell-only fraction taken from the first time step / level. It is tiny, but only correct when the mask never changes, as for a land-sea mask.
  • A list of names, or a mapping such as {"sst": "static", "ice": True}, restricts the fractions to selected variables.

Fractions are mostly exactly 0 or 1 and compress well; in a test with 8 time steps the full-shape fractions added about 7% to the store, the static ones under 1%. This mirrors the ocean_fraction variables of the nextGEMS HEALPix output.

items.title: Output metadata and CRS convention
items.text: Every output dataset carries the same metadata, written and read in one place: the grid_doctor.metadata package. Code that produces data builds a HealpixMetadata and calls its apply method; code that reads data calls HealpixMetadata.from_dataset. Attribute names are spelled out nowhere else, so changing the stored layout never touches the code that writes or reads values.

items.title: CF grid mapping
items.text:
The grid is described with the healpix grid mapping introduced in CF-1.13:

crs: float64                      # scalar grid mapping variable
    grid_mapping_name: healpix
    indexing_scheme: nested       # or ring
    refinement_level: 10          # always written, level 0 included
cell: int64 (cell)                # HEALPix index coordinate
    standard_name: healpix_index
    units: 1
latitude, longitude: float64 (cell)
    standard_name: latitude / longitude
    units: degrees_north / degrees_east

Every variable along cell carries grid_mapping = "crs", and the global Conventions attribute names CF-1.13 (any other convention in the source's Conventions, such as CMIP-6.2, is kept). nside = 2**refinement_level is not stored; it follows from the level. CF also defines nuniq and `zuniq as possible indexing_scheme; grid-doctor does not write them, so they are rejected rather than half supported.

CF identifies the index coordinate by its standard_name, not by its name, so the dimension stays cell, the name used across the HEALPix tooling of the km-scale hackathons. The standard name healpix_index was accepted in standard name table v94 (cf-convention/vocabularies#290). A generic name for all discrete global grid systems was proposed in that discussion and moved to cf-convention discussion #447, which is still open; should it be adopted, only one constant changes.

xdggs reads this layout with xdggs.decode(ds, convention="cf"). The geometry is spherical, which is also what xdggs and healpix-geo assume when no earth_radius is given.

items.title: grid-doctor attributes
items.text:
Attribute Description grid_doctor_metadata_version Version of this metadata layout (currently 1) grid_doctor_version Package version that produced the data grid_doctor_method conservative, nearest, binned-mean, ... (also per variable for binned data) grid_doctor_coarsened_from_level Level the values were coarsened from: the finest level for pyramids, the input level for coarsen_healpix (coarsened levels only) grid_doctor_coarsen_mode mean or mode (coarsened levels only) grid_doctor_min_valid_fraction Threshold below which cells were set to NaN: cumulative over finest-level cells for mean, per coarsening step for mode (coarsened levels only) grid_doctor_sparse 1 when cell holds a subset of cell indices (region selections, sparse binning) grid_doctor_implicit_coords 1 when cell/latitude/longitude were omitted (see below)

The crs convention is also what the gridlook viewer uses (grid_mapping_name == "healpix") to detect and render HEALPix datasets.

items.title: Pyramids in one store
items.text:
save_pyramid(..., structure="multiscales") writes a pyramid as one datatree, one group per level (level_<n>). Every level group carries the CF metadata above, so tools that only read a single group work unchanged. The root group carries the pyramid-wide attributes (source attributes, Conventions, grid-doctor version and method) and describes the levels with two Zarr conventions:

  • multiscales v0.1 lists the levels in layout, finest first. A coarsened level names the level it was coarsened from in derived_from, with transform.scale = [2**Δlevel] (the factor by which cell edges grow) and the resampling_method (average or mode).
  • dggs v1 describes each level's grid inside its layout entry: the source level carries the full object (name, refinement_level, indexing_scheme, spatial_dimension, coordinate), derived levels only what changes, usually just refinement_level. Stores with implicit coordinates omit coordinate, which the convention defines as covering the full sphere.
"multiscales": {
  "layout": [
    {"asset": "level_10", "dggs": {"name": "healpix", "refinement_level": 10,
      "indexing_scheme": "nested", "spatial_dimension": "cell",
      "coordinate": "cell", "compression": "none"}},
    {"asset": "level_9", "derived_from": "level_10",
      "transform": {"scale": [2.0]}, "dggs": {"refinement_level": 9}}
  ],
  "resampling_method": "average"
}

Both conventions are young: multiscales is a pilot with breaking changes expected before v1, and embedding dggs objects in layout entries follows a proposal that is not merged yet (zarr-conventions/dggs#25). The encoding therefore lives in one module (grid_doctor/metadata/_multiscales.py, with the pinned versions), and the tests validate it against the published schemas. Flat pyramids (one store per level) have no root group and carry only the per-level CF metadata.

items.title: Storage format
items.text:
Pyramids are written as Zarr stores with consolidated metadata, by default one store per level (level_0.zarr, level_1.zarr, …), or all levels in one store with structure="multiscales" (see Pyramids in one store). The default format is Zarr v2, and zarr_format=3 writes v3. Zarr v2 is the default because ecosystem support for v3 is still maturing: client libraries such as zarr-python, zarr-js (used by gridlook and similar web viewers), xarray, and zarrita have stable, well-tested v2 implementations, while v3 support varies in completeness. The transition to v3 is planned once the client ecosystem has converged.

Zarr's chunked, cloud-native layout enables byte-range reads from S3 without downloading entire files, which is essential for interactive visualisation where only a single chunk of a single variable at a single level needs to be fetched.

items.title: High-level regional datasets: implicit coordinates
items.text:
Small-area datasets at very high levels (16 and beyond) keep the dense global convention (cell position equals cell index) but stop materialising what the index already implies. Above level 10 (WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL), stores are written without cell/latitude/longitude coordinate arrays: at level 16 those two float64 arrays would cost ~800 GB while the regional payload is megabytes, and unlike the data variables they are never fill values, so empty-chunk elision cannot help. Such stores carry grid_doctor_implicit_coords = 1, retain the crs grid mapping, and remain byte-identical in layout to an ordinary dense store. Without the cell coordinate they lack the variable CF identifies by standard_name = "healpix_index", so generic CF tools cannot recognise them as HEALPix; grid-doctor's selectors can. Sparse datasets (region selections) always keep cell, since it records which cells they hold.

Access is region-driven through range selection. Nested ordering guarantees that every coarse-level parent corresponds to one contiguous fine-level index range, so a bounding-box query decomposes into a handful of contiguous reads that align one-to-one with power-of-four chunks. Coordinates are reconstructed on the fly for exactly the cells returned. Combined with fill_value = NaN and empty-chunk elision on the data variables, storage and access cost are proportional to the domain, not the globe, while cross-dataset and cross-level alignment stay a bit-shift (parent = id >> 2k) exactly as for every other nested HEALPix dataset.

Levels at or below the threshold within the same pyramid are written with materialised coordinates as usual, so coarse overview levels stay directly consumable by CF-aware viewers.

items.title: Performance: application backends
items.text:
The sparse weight-matrix multiplication supports three backends, selected automatically based on what is installed.

Batched SciPy (always available) reshapes all time steps into a single dense matrix and performs one sparse matmul, delegating to BLAS for the dense side. This is typically 10–50× faster than per-slice application.

Numba (optional) JIT-compiles a fused kernel that computes the weighted sum, NaN mask, and renormalization in a single pass over the sparse matrix structure. This halves memory traffic for single-slice workloads.

CuPy (optional) transfers the weight matrix to the GPU once and applies it via cuSPARSE. This is worthwhile for large target grids (HEALPix level 10+) with many time steps, where the transfer cost is amortised over the batch.

The backend can be overridden explicitly via backend="scipy", "numba", or "cupy" in any remapping call.

items.title: Chunked application and single-pass writes
items.text:
For dask-backed input, the regridded field is chunked along cell (cell_chunks, by default 4^10 cells). Rows of the weight matrix are independent, so each output chunk is computed from its own block of matrix rows; the blocks share the matrix memory instead of copying it. No task holds the whole HEALPix field, and the coarser levels keep the same chunking because every coarsening step only combines groups of 4 neighbouring cells.

Inside dask tasks the Numba kernels run single-threaded: dask already runs many tasks in parallel, and a multi-threaded kernel per task would start one thread team per task and exhaust the process thread limit on many-core nodes. Without dask, the multi-threaded kernels are used.

save_pyramid writes all levels in a single computation, so the regridding of each finest-level chunk runs exactly once and is shared by all coarser levels. Computing levels separately (for example pyramid[5].compute() followed by pyramid[4].compute()) regrids the source again each time; persist() the finest level when exploring interactively.

def get_parser(name: str, description: str | None = None) -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    """Create a parser preloaded with common grid-doctor options.

    Parameters
    ----------
    name:
        Program name shown in `--help` output.
    description:
        Optional one-line program description.

    Returns
    -------
    argparse.ArgumentParser
        Parser configured with common S3 and verbosity arguments.

    Examples
    --------
    ```python
    parser = get_parser("convert-icon", description="Build a HEALPix pyramid")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    ```
    """
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog=name,
        description=description,
        formatter_class=ArgFormatter,
    )
    parser.add_argument("--s3-bucket", help="S3 target bucket.", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--s3-endpoint", help="S3 endpoint URL.", required=True)
    parser.add_argument(
        "--s3-credentials-file",
        default=Path.home() / ".s3-credentials.json",
        help="Path to a JSON file with accessKey/secretKey.",
    )
    group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
    group.add_argument(
        "-v",
        "--verbose",
        action="count",
        default=0,
        help="Increase verbosity with repeated flags such as -v or -vv.",
    )
    return parser

def setup_logging(
    verbosity: int = 0,
    level: Union[int, str, None] = None,
    fmt: str = _DEFAULT_FORMAT,
    datefmt: str = _DEFAULT_DATE_FORMAT,
) -> None:
    """Configure the root handler and set the global log level.

    Call this **once** at program startup.

    Parameters
    ----------
    verbosity : int, optional
        Number of ``-v`` flags.  Each step moves one rung towards
        ``DEBUG`` on the verbosity ladder.
    level : int, str, or None, optional
        Explicit level; overrides *verbosity* when given.
    fmt : str, optional
        :mod:`logging` format string.
    datefmt : str, optional
        Date format string.
    """
    if not logging.root.handlers:
        handler = logging.StreamHandler()
        handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(fmt, datefmt=datefmt))
        logging.root.addHandler(handler)

    if level is not None:
        set_level(level)
    else:
        global _current_index
        _current_index = _DEFAULT_INDEX + verbosity
        _current_index = max(0, min(_current_index, len(_LEVELS) - 1))
        _apply_level(_LEVELS[_current_index])

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
grid_doctor.config holds library-wide settings. A setting is resolved in this order, later ones winning:

  1. the built-in default,
  2. the environment variable GRID_DOCTOR_<SETTING> (read at import),
  3. assignment at runtime.
Setting Default Values Environment variable ellipsoid "sphere" "sphere", "WGS84" GRID_DOCTOR_ELLIPSOID weights_store None ($XDG_CACHE_HOME/grid-doctor/weights) local path, file:// or memory:// URL GRID_DOCTOR_WEIGHTS_STORE 
import grid_doctor as gd

gd.config.ellipsoid = "WGS84"  # HEALPix geometry on WGS84

with gd.config.set(ellipsoid="sphere", weights_store="/work/ab1234/weights"):
    ...  # restored after the block

Settings are process-wide: a with gd.config.set(...) block also affects other threads while it is open, and dask workers in other processes only see the environment variable.

ellipsoid applies to grids being created (regridding, binning, weight generation). The ellipsoid is recorded in the output (CF reference_ellipsoid_name, semi_major_axis and inverse_flattening for WGS84) and in weight files; reading, selecting from or coarsening existing data uses the recorded ellipsoid. HEALPix metadata or a weight file without these attributes is spherical. A dataset with no HEALPix metadata at all gets this setting when selecting from it with an explicit level=; coarsening requires the HEALPix metadata.

weights_store is where cached_weights and regrid_to_healpix look up and store weight files; see Weights Store. grid-doctor never guesses a scratch or project directory: point it at one yourself, for example on an HPC system where the home directory has a small quota.

@contextmanager
def set(**settings: Any) -> Iterator[None]:
    """Change settings inside a ``with`` block, restoring them afterwards.

    Raises
    ------
    AttributeError
        If a setting does not exist.
    ValueError
        If a value is invalid; no setting is changed then.
    """
    for name, value in settings.items():
        _check(name, value)
    module = sys.modules[__name__]
    previous = {name: getattr(module, name) for name in settings}
    try:
        for name, value in settings.items():
            setattr(module, name, value)
        yield
    finally:
        for name, value in previous.items():
            setattr(module, name, value)

Parameters:

required path str

required s3_options S3Options | None

HEALPix coordinates are a pure function of the cell index, and above roughly level 10 the arrays dwarf regional payloads (hundreds of GB at level 16, and they are never fill values, so chunk elision cannot help). "auto" (default) writes coordinates for levels up to :data:WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL and omits them above; True / False force either behaviour for all levels. Coordinate- less stores keep the crs grid mapping, are marked as having implicit coordinates (see HealpixMetadata), and are meant to be accessed through the region selectors (select_bbox, select_cells), which reconstruct coordinates for exactly the cells they return.

'auto' structure Literal['flat', 'multiscales']

separate stores ('flat'), or combine them into a datatree ('multiscales').

'flat' Source code in grid_doctor/io/_save.py 
def save_pyramid(
    pyramid: dict[int, xr.Dataset],
    path: str,
    s3_options: S3Options | None = None,
    *,
    mode: Literal["a", "w", "r+"] = "a",
    region: Literal["auto"] | Region = "auto",
    zarr_format: Literal[2, 3] = 2,
    encoding: PyramidEncoding | None = None,
    write_coords: bool | Literal["auto"] = "auto",
    structure: Literal["flat", "multiscales"] = "flat",
) -> None:
    """Write a HEALPix pyramid to Zarr stores on S3 or local disk.

    Each level is stored below ``"<path>/level_<level>.zarr"``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pyramid:
        Mapping of HEALPix level to dataset.
    path:
        Target prefix.  An ``"s3://bucket/pyramid"`` URL writes to S3; any
        other value is treated as a local directory path.
    s3_options:
        Options forwarded to :class:`s3fs.S3FileSystem`.  Only used for S3
        targets; ignored (and optional) for local paths.
    mode:
        Zarr write mode.
    region:
        Region writes for partial updates.
    zarr_format:
        Zarr format version.
    encoding:
        Per-level encoding dictionaries.
    write_coords:
        Whether to materialise the ``cell``/``latitude``/``longitude``
        coordinate arrays in the store.  HEALPix coordinates are a pure
        function of the cell index, and above roughly level 10 the
        arrays dwarf regional payloads (hundreds of GB at level 16, and
        they are never fill values, so chunk elision cannot help).
        ``"auto"`` (default) writes coordinates for levels up to
        :data:`WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL` and omits them above; ``True`` /
        ``False`` force either behaviour for all levels.  Coordinate-
        less stores keep the ``crs`` grid mapping, are marked as having
        implicit coordinates (see
        [`HealpixMetadata`][grid_doctor.metadata.HealpixMetadata]), and are
        meant to be accessed through the region selectors
        ([`select_bbox`][grid_doctor.select_bbox],
        [`select_cells`][grid_doctor.select_cells]), which reconstruct
        coordinates for exactly the cells they return.
    structure: Specify whether to write the datasets in the pyramid to
        separate stores ('flat'), or combine them into a datatree
        ('multiscales').
    """
    fs = get_filesystem(path, s3_options)

    if structure == "multiscales":
        _save_multiscale(
            pyramid,
            path,
            fs,
            mode,
            region,
            zarr_format,
            encoding,
            write_coords,
        )
        return
    # Stores are initialised per level; the data of all levels is written
    # in one pass (see grid_doctor.io._zarr for why).
    deferred: list[DeferredWrite] = []
    encoding = encoding or {}
    for level, dataset in pyramid.items():
        dataset = maybe_drop_coordinates(dataset, level, write_coords, WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL)
        store_name = f"level_{level}"
        root_path = f"{path}/{store_name}.zarr"
        store = get_store(root_path, fs)
        logger.info("Writing HEALPix to %s", store)
        zarr_options = get_zarr_options(mode, zarr_format, encoding.get(level, None))

        if region == "auto":
            dataset.to_zarr(store, **zarr_options)  # type: ignore[call-overload]
            written, write_region = dataset, None
        else:
            # Fill in the region of data.
            written = prepare_region_dataset(dataset, region)
            written.to_zarr(  # type: ignore[call-overload]
                store,
                region=region,
                **zarr_options,
            )
            write_region = region
        deferred.extend(
            deferred_writes(
                written,
                store,
                encoding=zarr_options.get("encoding"),
                region=write_region,
                zarr_format=zarr_format,
            )
        )
    store_all(deferred)

def chunk_for_target_store_size(
    *,
    level: int,
    dtype: npt.DTypeLike = "float32",
    target_stored_mib: float = 16.0,
    compression_ratio: float = 2.0,
    access: Literal["time_series", "map"] = "map",
    ntime: int | None = None,
    max_time_chunk: int | None = None,
    max_cell_chunk: int | None = None,
) -> dict[str, int]:
    """
    Compute (time, cell) chunks for a HEALPix dataset.

    Parameters
    ----------
    level
        HEALPix order / level.
    dtype
        Variable dtype.
    target_stored_mib
        Desired approximate compressed chunk size on disk.
    compression_ratio
        Estimated ratio:
            uncompressed_bytes / compressed_bytes
    access
        "map" or "time_series".
    ntime
        Total time size. Needed for time_series mode unless max_time_chunk is given.
    max_time_chunk
        Optional cap for time chunk.
    max_cell_chunk
        Optional cap for cell chunk.

    Returns
    -------
    dict[str, int]
        Chunk sizes, e.g. {"time": 5, "cell": 786432}.
    """
    nside = 2**level
    ncell = 12 * nside * nside
    itemsize = np.dtype(dtype).itemsize

    target_stored_bytes = int(target_stored_mib * 1024 * 1024)
    target_uncompressed_bytes = int(target_stored_bytes * compression_ratio)

    if access == "map":
        cell_chunk = ncell if max_cell_chunk is None else min(ncell, max_cell_chunk)
        time_chunk = max(1, target_uncompressed_bytes // (itemsize * cell_chunk))
        return {"time": int(time_chunk), "cell": int(cell_chunk)}

    if access == "time_series":
        if max_time_chunk is not None:
            time_chunk = max_time_chunk
        elif ntime is not None:
            time_chunk = ntime
        else:
            raise ValueError("For access='time_series', provide either ntime or max_time_chunk.")

        if ntime is not None:
            time_chunk = min(time_chunk, ntime)

        cell_chunk = max(1, target_uncompressed_bytes // (itemsize * time_chunk))
        cell_chunk = min(cell_chunk, ncell)

        if max_cell_chunk is not None:
            cell_chunk = min(cell_chunk, max_cell_chunk)

        return {"time": int(time_chunk), "cell": int(cell_chunk)}

    raise ValueError(f"Unsupported access mode: {access!r}")

items.title: grid_doctor.metadata
items.text:
Metadata of grid-doctor datasets, written and read in one place.

Every attribute, coordinate name and grid mapping grid-doctor stores is defined in this package. Code that produces data builds a HealpixMetadata and calls apply; code that reads data calls HealpixMetadata.from_dataset. Changing the stored layout therefore never touches the write sites.

  • _grid: HealpixGrid, the grid itself (level, indexing scheme, figure of the earth).
  • _provenance: Provenance, how the values were produced.
  • _cf: the CF-1.13 healpix grid mapping spelling of a grid.
  • _dataset: HealpixMetadata, which combines the above and applies it to a dataset.
  • _multiscales: PyramidMetadata, the layout of a pyramid stored as one datatree, spelled with the Zarr multiscales and dggs conventions.
  • _pyramid: attributes of such a datatree's root group.
  • _keys: every stored name.

The written layout is CF-1.13: a scalar crs grid mapping variable (grid_mapping_name = "healpix", indexing_scheme, refinement_level), an integer cell index coordinate with standard_name = "healpix_index", and grid_mapping = "crs" on every variable along cell. xdggs.decode(ds, convention="cf") reads it. Pyramids written as one datatree additionally describe their levels on the root group (see PyramidMetadata).

Writes

  • a scalar crs grid mapping coordinate (replacing any existing one),
  • CF attributes on the cell index coordinate and the latitude/longitude coordinates, where present,
  • grid_mapping = "crs" on every variable along cell,
  • the global Conventions, provenance and layout attributes.

def apply(self, ds: xr.Dataset) -> xr.Dataset:
    """Return *ds* with all grid-doctor metadata written.

    Writes

    - a scalar ``crs`` grid mapping coordinate (replacing any
      existing one),
    - CF attributes on the ``cell`` index coordinate and the
      ``latitude``/``longitude`` coordinates, where present,
    - ``grid_mapping = "crs"`` on every variable along ``cell``,
    - the global ``Conventions``, provenance and layout attributes.

    Global attributes owned by grid-doctor are rewritten from this
    object, so stale values copied from an input dataset never
    survive.  Coordinate *values* are left to the caller.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        When the ``cell`` dimension or coordinate contradicts the
        grid or the layout.
    """
    self._check_layout(ds)
    crs = xr.DataArray(np.float64(0.0), attrs=grid_mapping_attrs(self.grid))
    # A shallow copy owns its attribute dicts, so *ds* is left untouched.
    result = ds.copy(deep=False).drop_vars(CRS_VAR, errors="ignore")
    result = result.assign_coords({CRS_VAR: crs})

    coord_attrs = ((CELL_DIM, INDEX_ATTRS), (LAT_VAR, LAT_ATTRS), (LON_VAR, LON_ATTRS))
    for coord, attrs in coord_attrs:
        if coord in result.coords:
            result[coord].attrs.update(attrs)

    for var in result.data_vars.values():
        if CELL_DIM in var.dims:
            var.attrs["grid_mapping"] = CRS_VAR

    global_attrs: dict[Hashable, object] = {
        key: value for key, value in result.attrs.items() if key not in OWNED_GLOBAL_ATTRS
    }
    global_attrs["Conventions"] = merge_conventions(ds.attrs.get("Conventions"))
    global_attrs[METADATA_VERSION_ATTR] = METADATA_VERSION
    global_attrs.update(self.provenance.to_attrs())
    if self.sparse:
        global_attrs[SPARSE_ATTR] = 1
    if self.implicit_coords:
        global_attrs[IMPLICIT_COORDS_ATTR] = 1
    result.attrs = global_attrs
    return result

def from_dataset(cls, ds: xr.Dataset) -> HealpixMetadata:
    """Read the metadata written by [`apply`][grid_doctor.metadata.HealpixMetadata.apply].

def __post_init__(self) -> None:
    """Check that every ``derived_from`` points to a described level."""
    assets = {level.asset: level for level in self.levels}
    if len(assets) != len(self.levels):
        raise ValueError("Pyramid levels must have unique assets.")
    for level in self.levels:

            continue
        source = assets.get(level.derived_from)
        if source is None or source.grid is None or level.grid is None:
            raise ValueError(

                "which is not a HEALPix level of this pyramid."

@classmethod
def from_pyramid(cls, pyramid: Mapping[int, xr.Dataset]) -> PyramidMetadata:
    """Describe *pyramid* (``{level: dataset}``) from its levels' metadata.

    A level is derived from the level its provenance names in
    ``coarsened_from_level``, when that level is part of the
    pyramid.  Levels without HEALPix metadata are listed by path.
    """
    levels: list[PyramidLevel] = []
    for level in sorted(pyramid, reverse=True):
        ds = pyramid[level]
        asset = level_group(level)
        if not has_healpix_metadata(ds):
            levels.append(PyramidLevel(asset=asset, grid=None, coordinate=None))
            continue
        metadata = HealpixMetadata.from_dataset(ds)
        source = metadata.provenance.coarsened_from_level
        derived = source is not None and source != level and source in pyramid
        mode = metadata.provenance.coarsen_mode
        levels.append(
            PyramidLevel(
                asset=asset,
                grid=metadata.grid,
                coordinate=CELL_DIM if CELL_DIM in ds.variables else None,
                derived_from=(level_group(source) if derived and source is not None else None),
                resampling_method=(RESAMPLING_METHODS.get(mode, mode) if derived and mode else None),
            )
        )
    return cls(levels=tuple(levels))

def to_attrs(self) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Return the ``zarr_conventions`` and ``multiscales`` attributes."""
    assets = {level.asset: level for level in self.levels}
    methods = {level.resampling_method for level in self.levels if level.derived_from is not None}
    shared_method = methods.pop() if len(methods) == 1 else None

    layout: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for level in self.levels:
        entry: dict[str, object] = {"asset": level.asset}
        if level.derived_from is not None and level.grid is not None:
            source = assets[level.derived_from]
            assert source.grid is not None  # checked in __post_init__
            entry["derived_from"] = level.derived_from
            entry["transform"] = {"scale": [float(2 ** (source.grid.level - level.grid.level))]}
            if level.resampling_method is not None and shared_method is None:
                entry["resampling_method"] = level.resampling_method
            entry["dggs"] = _changed_dggs(_dggs_object(source), _dggs_object(level))
        elif level.grid is not None:
            entry["dggs"] = _dggs_object(level)
        layout.append(entry)

    multiscales: dict[str, object] = {"layout": layout}
    if shared_method is not None:
        multiscales["resampling_method"] = shared_method
    conventions = [MULTISCALES_CONVENTION.to_dict()]
    if any(level.grid is not None for level in self.levels):

@classmethod
def from_attrs(cls, attrs: Mapping[Hashable, object]) -> PyramidMetadata:
    """Read the layout written by [`to_attrs`][grid_doctor.metadata.PyramidMetadata.to_attrs].

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        When *attrs* have no ``multiscales`` layout or describe a
        grid other than HEALPix.
    """
    multiscales = attrs.get("multiscales")
    if not isinstance(multiscales, Mapping) or not isinstance(multiscales.get("layout"), list):
        raise ValueError("Attributes have no `multiscales` layout.")
    entries: dict[str, Mapping[str, object]] = {}
    for entry in multiscales["layout"]:
        if not isinstance(entry, Mapping) or not isinstance(entry.get("asset"), str):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid multiscales layout entry: {entry!r}.")
        entries[entry["asset"]] = entry
    default_method = multiscales.get("resampling_method")

    resolved: dict[str, dict[str, object] | None] = {}

    def resolve(asset: str, seen: frozenset[str] = frozenset()) -> dict[str, object] | None:
        if asset in resolved:
            return resolved[asset]
        if asset in seen or asset not in entries:
            raise ValueError(f"Cannot resolve the dggs object of level {asset!r}.")
        entry = entries[asset]
        dggs = entry.get("dggs")
        source = entry.get("derived_from")
        if not isinstance(dggs, Mapping):
            result = None
        elif isinstance(source, str) and "name" not in dggs:
            base = resolve(source, seen | {asset})
            result = None if base is None else {**base, **dggs}
        else:
            result = dict(dggs)
        resolved[asset] = result
        return result

    levels = []
    for asset, entry in entries.items():
        dggs = resolve(asset)
        source = entry.get("derived_from")
        method = entry.get("resampling_method", default_method if source else None)
        levels.append(
            PyramidLevel(
                asset=asset,
                grid=None if dggs is None else _grid_from_dggs(dggs),
                coordinate=None if dggs is None else _optional_str(dggs.get("coordinate")),
                derived_from=source if isinstance(source, str) else None,
                resampling_method=_optional_str(method),
            )
        )
    return cls(levels=tuple(levels))

def merge_conventions(existing: object) -> str:

    Any ``CF-x.y`` token is replaced by the version grid-doctor writes;

items.title: Parallel writes
items.text:
Functions and data classes for writing a pyramid with many independent workers, for example as an HPC array job. The workflow is

  1. init_pyramid_store creates empty level stores and returns a PyramidManifest with one WriteTask per unit of work,
  2. every worker calls write_pyramid_task for its task,
  3. check_pyramid_store reports whether all tasks finished.

The Parallel writes recipe explains the design, the manifest format and a complete reflow workflow.

Create empty pyramid stores and plan the work to fill them.

This is step one of a fan-out write. It writes, for every level, "<path>/level_<level>.zarr" with all metadata, encodings and coordinates, but none of the (lazy) data variables, and returns a PyramidManifest that splits the remaining work into independent WriteTask units. Hand each task to one worker, which calls write_pyramid_task; afterwards check_pyramid_store tells whether everything was written. The manifest is also stored as "<path>/_grid_doctor/manifest.json".

No data is computed (apart from coordinates and materialise), so the init is cheap even for stores with hundreds of thousands of chunks. The pyramid only needs the right shapes, dtypes, chunks and attributes; it can be built lazily from the full source.

What happens when path already holds a pyramid is controlled by if_exists; by default the init refuses, so a second run cannot destroy the stores of a first one by accident.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pyramid dict[int, Dataset]

Mapping of HEALPix level to dataset, typically the lazy result of create_healpix_pyramid.

required path str

Target prefix. An "s3://bucket/pyramid" URL writes to S3; any other value is treated as a local directory path.

required s3_options S3Options | None

Options forwarded to :class:s3fs.S3FileSystem. Only used for S3 targets; ignored (and optional) for local paths. Never stored in the manifest.

None zarr_format Literal[2, 3]

Zarr format version.

2 encoding PyramidEncoding | None

Per-level encoding dictionaries. Chunking always follows the dask chunks of the pyramid (first chunk along each dimension).

None write_coords bool | Literal['auto']

Whether to materialise the cell/latitude/longitude coordinate arrays in the store. HEALPix coordinates are a pure function of the cell index, and above roughly level 10 the arrays dwarf regional payloads (hundreds of GB at level 16, and they are never fill values, so chunk elision cannot help). "auto" (default) writes coordinates for levels up to :data:WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL and omits them above; True / False force either behaviour for all levels. Coordinate- less stores keep the crs grid mapping, are marked as having implicit coordinates (see HealpixMetadata), and are meant to be accessed through the region selectors (select_bbox, select_cells), which reconstruct coordinates for exactly the cells they return.

'auto' materialise list[str] | None

Data variables to compute and write completely during the init, e.g. small static fields. They are not part of any task.

None structure Literal['flat', 'multiscales']

"flat" (default) writes one store per level, "<path>/level_<level>.zarr", and plans the fan-out tasks. "multiscales" writes the template of a single datatree store at path (one group per level) and returns None: fan-out tasks are not supported for it yet, so split, variables_per_task and if_exists="resume" are rejected, and an existing store at path is overwritten. Fill it with save_pyramid and structure="multiscales".

'flat' split Mapping[str, int] | None

Task size per dimension in index units, e.g. {"time": 24} for tasks of 24 time steps. Sizes are rounded up to a multiple of the zarr chunk (or shard) size along that dimension, taken over all variables and levels, so no two tasks ever write to the same chunk. Several dimensions give the cartesian product of their regions. Splitting along cell is not supported. None (default) plans one task per group of variables, covering the whole store.

None variables_per_task int | None

Maximum number of variables per task. None (default) keeps all variables that share split dimensions and levels in one task, so the regridding they share is computed once per region.

None if_exists IfExists

What to do if path already has a manifest, level stores, or the remains of an interrupted init:

  • "error" (default): raise StoreExistsError.
  • "resume": if the stored manifest was planned exactly as this call would plan it (same path, levels, array layouts, split and tasks), return it unchanged, with its manifest_id, and write nothing. Tasks that already finished keep their markers, so re-submitting a conversion after a time-out only redoes the missing tasks. Raises StoreExistsError listing the differences otherwise, or if there is no readable manifest to resume (e.g. the previous init was killed). Without anything at path it initialises normally.
  • "overwrite": re-initialise. All data is discarded, the result gets a new manifest_id, and tasks and markers of the previous manifest become invalid; workers still running for it fail with StaleTaskError. Only overwrite when no worker of a previous run may still be writing: grid-doctor does not lock the store, and a worker that is already writing can put its data into the new stores before it notices.

def init_pyramid_store(
    pyramid: dict[int, xr.Dataset],
    path: str,
    s3_options: S3Options | None = None,
    *,
    zarr_format: Literal[2, 3] = 2,
    encoding: PyramidEncoding | None = None,
    write_coords: bool | Literal["auto"] = "auto",
    materialise: list[str] | None = None,
    structure: Literal["flat", "multiscales"] = "flat",
    split: Mapping[str, int] | None = None,
    variables_per_task: int | None = None,
    if_exists: IfExists = "error",
) -> PyramidManifest | None:
    """Create empty pyramid stores and plan the work to fill them.

    This is step one of a fan-out write.  It writes, for every level,
    ``"<path>/level_<level>.zarr"`` with all metadata, encodings and
    coordinates, but none of the (lazy) data variables, and returns a
    [`PyramidManifest`][grid_doctor.PyramidManifest] that splits the
    remaining work into independent
    [`WriteTask`][grid_doctor.WriteTask] units.  Hand each task to one
    worker, which calls
    [`write_pyramid_task`][grid_doctor.write_pyramid_task]; afterwards
    [`check_pyramid_store`][grid_doctor.check_pyramid_store] tells
    whether everything was written.  The manifest is also stored as
    ``"<path>/_grid_doctor/manifest.json"``.

    No data is computed (apart from coordinates and *materialise*), so
    the init is cheap even for stores with hundreds of thousands of
    chunks.  The pyramid only needs the right shapes, dtypes, chunks and
    attributes; it can be built lazily from the full source.

    What happens when *path* already holds a pyramid is controlled by
    *if_exists*; by default the init refuses, so a second run cannot
    destroy the stores of a first one by accident.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pyramid:
        Mapping of HEALPix level to dataset, typically the lazy result
        of [`create_healpix_pyramid`][grid_doctor.create_healpix_pyramid].
    path:
        Target prefix.  An ``"s3://bucket/pyramid"`` URL writes to S3; any
        other value is treated as a local directory path.
    s3_options:
        Options forwarded to :class:`s3fs.S3FileSystem`.  Only used for S3
        targets; ignored (and optional) for local paths.  Never stored in
        the manifest.
    zarr_format:
        Zarr format version.
    encoding:
        Per-level encoding dictionaries.  Chunking always follows the
        dask chunks of the pyramid (first chunk along each dimension).
    write_coords:
        Whether to materialise the ``cell``/``latitude``/``longitude``
        coordinate arrays in the store.  HEALPix coordinates are a pure
        function of the cell index, and above roughly level 10 the
        arrays dwarf regional payloads (hundreds of GB at level 16, and
        they are never fill values, so chunk elision cannot help).
        ``"auto"`` (default) writes coordinates for levels up to
        :data:`WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL` and omits them above; ``True`` /
        ``False`` force either behaviour for all levels.  Coordinate-
        less stores keep the ``crs`` grid mapping, are marked as having
        implicit coordinates (see
        [`HealpixMetadata`][grid_doctor.metadata.HealpixMetadata]), and are
        meant to be accessed through the region selectors
        ([`select_bbox`][grid_doctor.select_bbox],
        [`select_cells`][grid_doctor.select_cells]), which reconstruct
        coordinates for exactly the cells they return.
    materialise:
        Data variables to compute and write completely during the init,
        e.g. small static fields.  They are not part of any task.
    structure:
        ``"flat"`` (default) writes one store per level,
        ``"<path>/level_<level>.zarr"``, and plans the fan-out tasks.
        ``"multiscales"`` writes the template of a single datatree store
        at *path* (one group per level) and returns ``None``: fan-out
        tasks are not supported for it yet, so *split*,
        *variables_per_task* and ``if_exists="resume"`` are rejected, and
        an existing store at *path* is overwritten.  Fill it with
        [`save_pyramid`][grid_doctor.save_pyramid] and
        ``structure="multiscales"``.
    split:
        Task size per dimension in index units, e.g. ``{"time": 24}``
        for tasks of 24 time steps.  Sizes are rounded **up** to a
        multiple of the zarr chunk (or shard) size along that dimension,
        taken over all variables and levels, so no two tasks ever write
        to the same chunk.  Several dimensions give the cartesian
        product of their regions.  Splitting along ``cell`` is not
        supported.  ``None`` (default) plans one task per group of
        variables, covering the whole store.
    variables_per_task:
        Maximum number of variables per task.  ``None`` (default) keeps
        all variables that share split dimensions and levels in one
        task, so the regridding they share is computed once per region.
    if_exists:
        What to do if *path* already has a manifest, level stores, or the
        remains of an interrupted init:

        - ``"error"`` (default): raise
          [`StoreExistsError`][grid_doctor.io.StoreExistsError].
        - ``"resume"``: if the stored manifest was planned exactly as
          this call would plan it (same path, levels, array layouts,
          split and tasks), return it unchanged, with its
          ``manifest_id``, and write nothing.  Tasks that already
          finished keep their markers, so re-submitting a conversion
          after a time-out only redoes the missing tasks.  Raises
          [`StoreExistsError`][grid_doctor.io.StoreExistsError] listing
          the differences otherwise, or if there is no readable
          manifest to resume (e.g. the previous init was killed).
          Without anything at *path* it initialises normally.
        - ``"overwrite"``: re-initialise.  All data is discarded, the
          result gets a new ``manifest_id``, and tasks and markers of the
          previous manifest become invalid; workers still running for
          it fail with ``StaleTaskError``.  Only overwrite when no
          worker of a previous run may still be writing: grid-doctor
          does not lock the store, and a worker that is already writing
          can put its data into the new stores before it notices.

    Returns
    -------
    PyramidManifest or None
        Store layout and tasks.  JSON-serialisable via
        ``manifest.to_json()`` and accepted directly as a reflow task
        result.  ``None`` for ``structure="multiscales"``.

    Examples
    --------
    ```python
    pyramid = create_healpix_pyramid(ds, max_level=9)
    manifest = init_pyramid_store(pyramid, "/scratch/out", split={"time": 24})
    for task in manifest.tasks:  # one array-job element each
        write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task)
    check_pyramid_store(manifest).raise_if_incomplete()
    ```
    """
    if if_exists not in ("error", "resume", "overwrite"):
        raise ValueError(f"if_exists must be 'error', 'resume' or 'overwrite', got {if_exists!r}")
    if structure not in ("flat", "multiscales"):
        raise ValueError(f"structure must be 'flat' or 'multiscales', got {structure!r}")
    materialise = list(materialise or [])
    if structure == "multiscales":
        unsupported = [
            name
            for name, given in (
                ("split", split is not None),
                ("variables_per_task", variables_per_task is not None),
                ("if_exists='resume'", if_exists == "resume"),
            )
            if given
        ]
        if unsupported:
            raise NotImplementedError(
                f"{', '.join(unsupported)} not supported for "
                "structure='multiscales' yet; use structure='flat' for fan-out "
                "writes"
            )
        _init_multiscales(
            pyramid,
            path,
            s3_options,
            zarr_format=zarr_format,
            encoding=encoding,
            write_coords=write_coords,
            materialise=materialise,
        )
        return None

    # Workers rebuild store paths from the manifest; keep them identical.
    path = path.rstrip("/")
    existing = inspect_target(path, s3_options, [f"level_{level}.zarr" for level in pyramid])
    if existing.exists and if_exists == "error":
        raise StoreExistsError(
            f"{path} already holds a pyramid ({existing.describe()}).  Pass "
            "if_exists='resume' to continue it or if_exists='overwrite' to "
            "start over."
        )
    if existing.exists and if_exists == "resume":
        if existing.manifest is None:
            raise StoreExistsError(
                f"cannot resume {path}: there is no readable manifest "
                f"({existing.describe()}).  Use if_exists='overwrite'."
            )
        templates = {
            level: maybe_drop_coordinates(ds, level, write_coords, WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL)
            for level, ds in pyramid.items()
        }
        return resume_init(
            existing.manifest,
            path,
            templates,
            {level: [str(k) for k in ds.data_vars if str(k) not in materialise] for level, ds in templates.items()},
            s3_options,
            zarr_format=zarr_format,
            split=split,
            variables_per_task=variables_per_task,
            materialised=[m for m in materialise if m in {str(v) for ds in pyramid.values() for v in ds}],
        )
    fs = get_filesystem(path, s3_options)
    begin_init(path, s3_options)
    level_specs: dict[int, LevelSpec] = {}
    for level, dataset in pyramid.items():
        template, combined_encoding = prepare_template(
            dataset,
            level,
            write_coords=write_coords,
            max_level_to_auto_write_coords=WRITE_COORDS_MAX_LEVEL,
            encoding=encoding,
            materialise=materialise,
        )
        task_vars = [str(k) for k in template.data_vars if str(k) not in materialise]
        store_name = f"level_{level}.zarr"
        root_path = f"{path}/{store_name}"
        store = get_store(root_path, fs)
        logger.info("Writing HEALPix to %s", root_path)
        zarr_options = get_zarr_options("w", zarr_format, combined_encoding)
        template.to_zarr(store, **zarr_options)  # type: ignore[call-overload]
        level_specs[level] = describe_level(
            level,
            store_name,
            store,
            template,
            task_vars,
            zarr_format=zarr_format,
        )

    unknown = sorted(set(materialise) - {str(v) for ds in pyramid.values() for v in ds})
    if unknown:
        logger.warning("materialise names unknown variables: %s", ", ".join(unknown))
    return finish_init(
        path,
        s3_options,
        [level_specs[lvl] for lvl in sorted(level_specs, reverse=True)],
        zarr_format=zarr_format,
        split=split,
        variables_per_task=variables_per_task,
        materialised=[m for m in materialise if m not in unknown],
    )
