def __post_init__(self) -> None:
    """Lowercase every string field, so one set of weights has one path, and validate them.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a field cannot appear in a weight reference.
    """
    for name in self.__dataclass_fields__:
        value = getattr(self, name)
        if isinstance(value, str):
            object.__setattr__(self, name, value.lower())
    valid = {
        "method": self.method in get_args(RemapMethod),
        "level": type(self.level) is int and 0 <= self.level <= MAX_LEVEL,
        "key": isinstance(self.key, str) and _SHA256_HEX.fullmatch(self.key) is not None,
        "grid": self.grid == GRID_MAPPING_NAME,
        "ellipsoid": self.ellipsoid in _REF_ELLIPSOIDS,
        "version": self.version == WEIGHTS_VERSION,
    }
    for name, ok in valid.items():
        if not ok:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid weight reference {name}: {getattr(self, name)!r}")

items.title: parse(path) classmethod
items.text:
Parse a relative weight file path, the inverse of path.

Raises: ValueError: If path does not follow the layout.

Source code in grid_doctor/weights.py 
@classmethod
def parse(cls, path: str) -> WeightsRef:
    """Parse a relative weight file path, the inverse of [`path`][grid_doctor.weights.WeightsRef.path].

    Raises:
        ValueError: If *path* does not follow the layout.
    """
    *dirs, file = path.strip("/").split("/")
    pairs = [d.partition("=") for d in dirs]
    values = {name: value for name, _, value in pairs}
    if (
        tuple(name for name, _, _ in pairs) != cls.HIERARCHY
        or any(sep != "=" for _, sep, _ in pairs)
        or not (values["version"].isdigit() and values["level"].isdigit())
        or not file.endswith(".nc")
    ):
        raise ValueError(f"Not a weight reference: {path!r}")
    try:
        return cls(
            method=cast(RemapMethod, values["method"]),
            level=int(values["level"]),
            key=file.removesuffix(".nc"),
            grid=values["grid"],
            ellipsoid=values["ellipsoid"],
            version=int(values["version"]),
        )
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise ValueError(f"Not a weight reference: {path!r} ({exc})") from None

def check_coverage(path: str | Path) -> None:
    """Raise when weight file *path* leaves HEALPix target cells unmapped.

    Repeats the check of ``ignore_unmapped=False`` for weights that were
    generated (and stored) with unmapped cells ignored. Files without the
    unmapped-cells attribute (older files) pass.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the file records unmapped target cells.
    """
    with xr.open_dataset(path) as ds:
        unmapped = int(ds.attrs.get(keys.UNMAPPED_CELLS_ATTR, 0))
    if unmapped:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{unmapped} HEALPix target cells of {path} are not covered by the source grid; "
            "pass ignore_unmapped=True to accept them as missing values."
        )

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
Worked examples from source data to a published HEALPix pyramid. The conversion recipes follow the same steps: open the data, get the weights (or bin the samples), build the pyramid and write it.

Recipe Source data Examples Structured grids Regular and curvilinear lat/lon grids ERA5, CMIP6 Unstructured grids Triangular meshes ICON Regional grids Limited-area and rotated-pole domains CORDEX Point data Swaths, stations, trajectories EarthCARE MSI, station networks

Two recipes cover what comes after or around the conversion:

  • Coarsening and averaging masked fields computes means and area integrals of fields with missing values consistently across pyramid levels.
  • Parallel writes splits the conversion of a large source into independent array-job tasks driven by a manifest, with a complete reflow workflow.

To read the published data, including stores without coordinate arrays, see Working with the data.

items.title: Coarsening and averaging masked fields
items.text:
Every HEALPix cell has the same area, so a complete field needs no area weights: its global mean is the plain mean over cells. This recipe is for fields that represent only part of a cell, because data is missing or because the field is ocean- or land-only.

It explains how to:

  • store valid fractions while building a pyramid;
  • retain physical ocean or land coverage separately from data validity;
  • find the appropriate support for a variable; and
  • use that support for global, regional, and zonal means, and area integrals.

The background is explained in Averaging over coarse levels.

items.title: Storing the valid fractions
items.text:
Fractions are written when the pyramid is created:

import grid_doctor as gd

# ds, level and weights_file as in the structured-grid recipe;
# store is the output directory or s3:// URL
pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(
    max_level=level,
    weights_path=weights_file,
    # land-sea masked SST: one cell-only fraction is enough;
    # sea ice changes over time and needs the full shape
    valid_fraction={"sst": "static", "siconc": True},
)
gd.save_pyramid(pyramid, store, mode="w")

Every level then contains sst_valid_fraction and siconc_valid_fraction (float32, between 0 and 1), linked from the data variables through the CF ancillary_variables attribute. A static fraction has only the cell dimension and broadcasts against all time steps.

items.title: Ocean and land fields: retaining physical coverage
items.text:
*_valid_fraction answers “where was this variable available?” It does not answer “how much of this cell is ocean or land?” Those are separate quantities at coastlines and where observations are missing. For an ocean-only or land-only variable, retain a continuous physical coverage variable as well:

Field Store Weight a spatial mean by Complete global field value no weight: value.mean("cell") Field with data gaps value, value_valid_fraction valid fraction Ocean-only field value, ocean fraction, valid-ocean fraction valid-ocean fraction Land-only field value, land fraction or land-sea mask, valid-land fraction valid-land fraction

Ocean fractions, land fractions, and land-sea masks are continuous fields

An ocean fraction, land fraction, or land-sea mask describes coverage, not a categorical land/ocean label. Coarsen any of them with coarsen_mode="mean"; using mode would discard partial coverage of coastal cells. If a value is valid throughout the ocean (or land), the corresponding physical fraction is also the correct weight.

Do not derive a production land or ocean fraction from whether a data variable is non-null. A validity mask cannot distinguish physical land or ocean from missing observations.

items.title: Building a pyramid for an ocean-only field
items.text:
create_healpix_pyramid can create valid fractions for ordinary masked fields, but it does not infer a physical ocean or land fraction. Build and coarsen a numerator and its coverage explicitly when both concepts matter. The EasyGEMS ocean-averaging example uses the same distinction between an ocean-only value and its physical coverage. The example below uses a sea-ice velocity ice_u, written \(v\) in the formulas:

Let \(v_i\) be the value in a finest-level child cell, \(f_i\) its physical ocean fraction, and \(w_i\) its valid-ocean fraction:

\[ w_i = \begin{cases} f_i, & \text{when } v_i \text{ is valid}, \\ 0, & \text{when } v_i \text{ is missing}. \end{cases} \]

For a parent \(p\) with \(k\) children (\(k = 4\) for one nested HEALPix step, or \(4^d\) for a direct reduction over \(d\) levels), coarsen the numeric numerator and coverage separately:

\[ N_p = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in p} v_i w_i, \qquad C_p = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in p} w_i, \qquad v_p = \frac{N_p}{C_p} \quad \text{where } C_p > 0. \]

The common \(1/k\) factor makes each result a fraction of the parent-cell area and cancels in the reconstructed value. A missing child contributes zero to both quantities. Thus \(v_p\) remains the mean over its valid ocean area, while \(C_p\) retains exactly how much of that area it represents. A spatial ocean mean then combines parent cells as

\[ \mu_\mathrm{ocean} = \frac{\sum_p v_p C_p}{\sum_p C_p}. \]

In the code, finest is the finest HEALPix level (for example the output of regrid_to_healpix), at level max_level; the loop builds the levels down to min_level.

import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

ice = finest.ice_u
ocean_fraction = finest.ocean_fraction_surface.fillna(0)
valid_ocean_fraction = ocean_fraction.where(ice.notnull(), 0).fillna(0)

state = xr.Dataset(
    {
        # Zero is safe here because coverage is zero for land and missing data.
        "ice_u_numerator": (ice * valid_ocean_fraction).fillna(0),
        "ice_u_coverage": valid_ocean_fraction,
        "ocean_fraction_surface": ocean_fraction,
    },
    attrs=finest.attrs.copy(),
)

def public_level(state: xr.Dataset) -> xr.Dataset:
    coverage = state.ice_u_coverage
    ice_u = state.ice_u_numerator / coverage.where(coverage > 0)
    # Link the value to its weights, so tools (and the helper further
    # below) find them.
    ice_u.attrs["ancillary_variables"] = "ice_u_valid_fraction"
    return xr.Dataset(
        {
            "ice_u": ice_u,
            "ice_u_valid_fraction": coverage,
            "ocean_fraction_surface": state.ocean_fraction_surface,
        },
        attrs=state.attrs.copy(),
    )

levels = {max_level: public_level(state)}
for level in range(max_level - 1, min_level - 1, -1):
    state = gd.coarsen_healpix(
        state, level, coarsen_mode="mean", min_valid_fraction=0.0
    )
    levels[level] = public_level(state)

The stored ice_u remains the mean velocity over the valid ocean part of a cell: a cell that is 20% ocean and has velocity 0.8 m/s stores 0.8 m/s, not 0.16 m/s. The separate ice_u_valid_fraction supplies its weight when cells are combined:

ocean_mean = ds.ice_u.weighted(ds.ice_u_valid_fraction.fillna(0)).mean("cell")

If the field is valid everywhere that is physically ocean, weight by ocean_fraction_surface instead.

items.title: Building a pyramid for a land-only field
items.text:
The same construction applies to a global land-only variable. Use a continuous land_fraction_surface (or a land-sea mask normalised to 0–1), and coarsen it with mean, never mode:

v = finest["land_variable"]  # replace with the ERA5-Land variable name
land_fraction = finest.land_fraction_surface.fillna(0)
valid_land_fraction = land_fraction.where(v.notnull(), 0).fillna(0)

state = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "v_numerator": (v * valid_land_fraction).fillna(0),
        "v_coverage": valid_land_fraction,
        "land_fraction_surface": land_fraction,
    },
    attrs=finest.attrs.copy(),
)

Coarsen and reconstruct it exactly as for ice_u. Store the public value, land_fraction_surface, and v_valid_fraction; weight a global mean by the latter, or by land_fraction_surface when data is valid everywhere on land. Do not infer physical land coverage from non-null values: they also reflect missing data.

items.title: Vertical dimensions
items.text:
Use a depth-specific physical fraction only when coverage really varies with depth. This is common for a three-dimensional ocean field, where the fraction must be on the same vertical grid and selected at the same depth before averaging:

to = ds.to.isel(time=0, depth_full=0)
weights = ds.ocean_fraction_depth_full.isel(depth_full=0)
ocean_mean = to.weighted(weights).mean("cell")

Leaving the ocean weights three-dimensional while selecting one data depth can broadcast arrays and yield a plausible but incorrect result.

For land only fields, soil variables on the other hand have a depth coordinate, but the physical land fraction normally remains cell-only: use the same land_fraction_surface for every soil layer. Only the valid fraction needs a depth dimension when availability differs between layers.

items.title: Finding the weights of a variable
items.text:
The ancillary_variables attribute names the fraction, so a small helper works for any variable, with or without fractions:

import xarray as xr

def valid_fraction(ds: xr.Dataset, name: str) -> xr.DataArray | None:
    """Return the valid-fraction weights of ``ds[name]``, if stored."""
    for candidate in ds[name].attrs.get("ancillary_variables", "").split():
        if candidate.endswith("_valid_fraction") and candidate in ds:
            return ds[candidate].fillna(0)
    return None


def weighted_mean(ds: xr.Dataset, name: str, dim: str = "cell") -> xr.DataArray:
    """Area mean over the valid part of ``ds[name]``."""
    weights = valid_fraction(ds, name)
    if weights is None:  # complete field: every cell counts fully
        return ds[name].mean(dim)
    return ds[name].weighted(weights).mean(dim)

items.title: Global mean and time series
items.text:
ds = xr.open_zarr(f"{store}/level_5.zarr")

global_sst = weighted_mean(ds, "sst")      # one value per time step
global_sst.plot()

The same call on any other level gives the same result, see checking consistency below.

items.title: Regional mean
items.text:
The region selectors keep all variables with a cell dimension, so the fractions are selected together with the data:

north_sea = ds.gd.select_bbox(lon=(-4.0, 9.0), lat=(51.0, 61.0))
regional_sst = weighted_mean(north_sea, "sst")

items.title: Zonal mean
items.text:
xarray's weighted does not combine with groupby, so form the weighted sums explicitly. Weights only count where the data is valid:

import numpy as np

bands = np.arange(-90, 91, 15)
latitude = ds["latitude"].compute()          # grouping needs loaded labels
weights = valid_fraction(ds, "sst").where(ds["sst"].notnull(), 0)
numerator = (ds["sst"].fillna(0) * weights).groupby_bins(latitude, bands).sum()
denominator = weights.groupby_bins(latitude, bands).sum()
zonal_sst = numerator / denominator          # NaN for bands without data

Stores above level 10 have no materialised latitude coordinate; use a level at or below 10 for zonal statistics, or the region selectors, which reconstruct coordinates for the cells they return.

items.title: Area integrals
items.text:
All cells of a level have the area \(4 \pi R^2 / n_\text{cells}\), so the valid area and area integrals are sums over the fractions:

R = 6371.0                                    # km, the sphere of the grid
cell_area = 4 * np.pi * R**2 / ds.sizes["cell"]

ocean_area = valid_fraction(ds, "sst").sum("cell") * cell_area
sst_integral = (ds["sst"] * valid_fraction(ds, "sst")).sum("cell") * cell_area

The valid area is identical on every level: a coarse cell has \(4^k\) times the area of a finest-level cell, and its fraction is the number of its valid finest-level cells divided by \(4^k\). The integral is too, as long as no cells were masked by min_valid_fraction (masked cells drop out of the sum, see pitfalls).

items.title: Checking consistency across levels
items.text:
for level in range(5, -1, -1):
    lvl = xr.open_zarr(f"{store}/level_{level}.zarr")
    print(level, weighted_mean(lvl, "sst").isel(time=0).values)

With min_valid_fraction=0 the printed means agree to rounding precision on every level.

items.title: Pitfalls
items.text:
• Plain means over coarse levels. ds["sst"].mean("cell") gives partly valid cells full weight and drifts from level to level. Use the weights whenever a field has missing values.
  • Cells masked by min_valid_fraction. A cell with less than min_valid_fraction (default 0.5) of its finest-level cells valid is NaN even though its fraction is positive. Weighted means skip it, so with the default threshold coarse-level means describe a slightly smaller area than the finest level. Build the pyramid with min_valid_fraction=0 if exact agreement across levels matters more than hiding sparsely covered cells. The threshold a level was built with is stored in its grid_doctor_min_valid_fraction attribute.
  • Static fractions for changing masks. "static" stores the mask of the first time step only. Use the full shape (True) for masks that change over time or height, such as sea ice or clouds.
  • Unweighted regional means. Domain-edge cells of regional datasets are partly valid on coarse levels too; weight them in the same way.

items.title: Unstructured grids (ICON)
items.text: This recipe converts ICON model output on a triangular mesh to a HEALPix pyramid. Unstructured grids are detected automatically; the weights are computed from the grid file and reused for every variable and time step.

items.title: Weights from the grid file
items.text:
Remapping from an unstructured grid needs the vertices of every cell, which ICON keeps in its grid file (clon_vertices, clat_vertices) and usually not in the data files. Compute the weights from the grid file:

import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

# The grid file has the cell centres and vertices, but no data variables.
grid_ds = xr.open_dataset("icon_grid_R02B07.nc")

level = gd.resolution_to_healpix_level(gd.get_latlon_resolution(grid_ds))
weights_file = gd.cached_weights(grid_ds, level=level, store="/path/to/weights")

The weight file is stored in the weights store. Later runs with the same grid, by you or by anyone using the same store, take it from there instead of computing it again.

items.title: Conversion
items.text:
With the weights, the data files are converted like structured grids:

ds = xr.open_mfdataset("icon_output_*.nc")

pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(max_level=level, weights_path=weights_file)

gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    "s3://my-bucket/icon/hourly",
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options("https://s3.example.org", "~/.s3-credentials.json"),
)

The cells of the data must be in the order of the grid file. ICON GRIB files read with cfgrib name the cell dimension values; rename it so the dimension is recognised:

ds = ds.rename_dims({"values": "cell"})

items.title: How grid detection works
items.text:
A dataset is treated as unstructured when

  • it has a dimension named cell, ncells, ncell or nCells, or
  • a data variable has the attribute CDI_grid_type = "unstructured".

The cell vertices are taken from clon_vertices/clat_vertices, lon_vertices/lat_vertices, lon_bnds/lat_bnds, or the CF bounds variables of the cell-centre coordinates.

items.title: Production runs
items.text: For a whole reanalysis or simulation, split the conversion into independent tasks for an HPC array job, see Parallel writes. The repository's scripts/icon-dream/ folder holds a complete conversion of the DWD ICON-DREAM reanalysis with reflow.

items.title: Parallel writes with a manifest
items.text:
save_pyramid writes a whole pyramid in one dask computation on one machine. That stops working when the source is too large for the memory or the wall-clock limit of a single job, for example decades of hourly data at HEALPix level 10 or above. The answer is to split the work into many small, independent jobs: one job creates empty stores and decides how the work is cut, an array job fills the stores in parallel, and a last job checks that nothing is missing.

grid-doctor supports exactly this pattern through a manifest:

flowchart LR
    A["init_pyramid_store()<br/>empty stores + manifest"] -->|"manifest.tasks"| B1["write_pyramid_task(task 0)"]
    A --> B2["write_pyramid_task(task 1)"]
    A --> B3["write_pyramid_task(task …)"]
    A --> B4["write_pyramid_task(task N)"]
    B1 --> C["check_pyramid_store()<br/>complete?"]
    B2 --> C
    B3 --> C
    B4 --> C
  1. Init (init_pyramid_store) writes every level store with its metadata, encodings and coordinates, but no data. It returns a PyramidManifest: the layout of the stores plus a list of WriteTask work units. Each task names the variables and the index region one worker has to write.
  2. Write (write_pyramid_task) is called once per task, by any number of workers, in any order, on any number of nodes. No locking is needed: tasks never share a zarr chunk.
  3. Check (check_pyramid_store) reports which tasks have finished and whether the stores still look like the manifest says. Missing tasks can be retried individually.

The manifest and the tasks are plain, frozen dataclasses that serialise to JSON. They can be returned from one reflow job and fed into the next one without any glue code, which is what the reflow section below shows.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
Everything in one process, to show the moving parts. On an HPC system each loop iteration would be one array-job element.

import xarray as xr
import grid_doctor as gd

source = xr.open_mfdataset("era5/tas_*.nc", chunks={"time": 24})
pyramid = source.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(max_level=9)  # lazy

# 1. Empty stores + plan: tasks of 72 time steps each.
manifest = gd.init_pyramid_store(pyramid, "/scratch/project/era5", split={"time": 72})
print(len(manifest.tasks), "tasks")

# 2. One call per task (this is what the array job does).
for task in manifest.tasks:
    gd.write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task)

# 3. Did everything arrive?
report = gd.check_pyramid_store(manifest)
print(report.summary())
report.raise_if_incomplete()

The result is identical, attribute for attribute and value for value, to what save_pyramid(pyramid, path, mode="w") would have written.

items.title: Manifest fields
items.text: Field Meaning schema_version Layout version of this JSON. A grid-doctor that does not know the version refuses to read it instead of guessing. manifest_id Random id created by every init. Every task and every completion marker carries it, which is how stale work is recognised after a re-init. path Pyramid root as passed to init_pyramid_store. zarr_format Zarr format (2 or 3) of all level stores. created UTC timestamp of the init. grid_doctor_version Version that wrote the manifest. split Effective task size per split dimension, after rounding (see planning). Empty when nothing was split. materialised Data variables the init wrote completely itself (materialise=). levels One entry per level, finest first. tasks All work units. Together they cover every data variable on every level exactly once.

items.title: Level fields
items.text:
Field Meaning level HEALPix refinement level. store Store name relative to path. coords Arrays the init wrote completely (coordinates, crs, materialised variables). Workers never touch them. data_vars Arrays that tasks write, with dims, full shape, on-disk dtype and chunks.

chunks is the write unit: the shard shape for sharded zarr v3 arrays, the chunk shape otherwise. It is read back from the store after the init, so it reflects what the stores really contain, not what was requested.

items.title: Task fields
items.text:
Field Meaning task_id Unique within the manifest; also the name of the completion marker. variables Data variables this task writes. region Half-open index range per split dimension, {"time": [0, 72]} means time indices 0 to 71. Dimensions that are not listed are written in full. An empty region means "the whole array" (variables without any split dimension). levels Levels the task writes, finest first. A task always covers all levels of its variables, because coarse levels are derived from the finest one.

Inside the manifest file the tasks omit the fields they share with the manifest. A task on its own (task.to_json()) also carries manifest_id, path and zarr_format, so that it is self-contained: a worker needs nothing but the task, the data and, for S3, credentials.

items.title: Where it is stored
items.text:
The init writes the manifest next to the level stores, and every finished task leaves a small marker there:

<path>/
├── level_9.zarr/
├── level_8.zarr/
├── level_7.zarr/
└── _grid_doctor/
    ├── init.json             # only while an init runs (or after it was killed)
    ├── manifest.json         # written last by the init
    └── done/
        ├── task-000000.json  # one marker per finished task
        └── ...

A marker records the task id, the manifest id, the host, the finish time and the elapsed seconds, which is handy when you want to know where and how long a task ran.

The manifest is written after all level stores exist, so its presence means the init finished. A re-init deletes the old manifest and all markers before touching the stores, so workers of an earlier run fail immediately instead of writing into the new stores.

init.json is written when an init starts and removed right after the manifest. It records the start time, host, process id and, inside a Slurm job, SLURM_JOB_ID. If it is still there without a manifest, the init was killed (time limit, scancel, node failure) or is still running, and the error messages of load_manifest, check_pyramid_store and init_pyramid_store say so, for example:

ManifestError: no manifest at /scratch/project/era5: an init started
2026-10-27T11:02:13+00:00 on host l40123 (Slurm job 4711) has not
finished; it is still running or was killed

items.title: Serialisation
items.text:
text = manifest.to_json()                     # str, pretty-printed
manifest = gd.PyramidManifest.from_json(text)

task_json = manifest.tasks[3].to_json()       # self-contained task
task = gd.WriteTask.from_json(task_json)

manifest = gd.load_manifest("/scratch/project/era5")  # read the stored copy

All classes are frozen dataclasses built only from str, int and tuple. That has two consequences:

  • reflow's manifest codec serialises them natively. A job can return a PyramidManifest, a WriteTask or list[WriteTask] and the next job receives the same object back, type and all.
  • They are hashable and compare by value, so task in done_tasks and using tasks as dictionary keys just work.

task.slices (or task.isel()) turns the region into a mapping that Dataset.isel understands: {"time": slice(0, 72)}.

items.title: Validation
items.text:
There is no separate JSON Schema file. Instead every object validates itself when it is created, in __post_init__. That matters because manifests and tasks arrive by three routes: parsed from JSON (from_json, load_manifest), rebuilt by reflow's codec (which calls the constructor directly and never goes through from_json), or built by hand. A JSON Schema would only cover the first one.

Each class checks its own fields:

Class Checks ArraySpec name is a valid array name; dims unique strings; shape integers ≥ 0; chunks integers ≥ 1; dims, shape and chunks of equal length. LevelSpec level ≥ 0; store is a plain name (no /, no leading .); unique data variables; no name both coordinate and data variable. WriteTask task_id and manifest_id are plain names (they become file names); zarr_format is 2 or 3; variables non-empty and unique; region entries well formed with 0 ≤ start ≤ stop; levels non-empty and unique. PyramidManifest schema_version is supported; split sizes ≥ 1 and not along cell; plus the consistency checks below.

The manifest additionally checks that its tasks fit its layout, which is the property parallel writes depend on:

  • every task's manifest_id, path and zarr_format match the manifest's, and task ids are unique;
  • every task level and variable exists, and region dimensions are split dimensions the variable actually has;
  • every region lies inside the array and starts and ends on write-unit boundaries (or at the array end);
  • for each data variable on each level, the task regions tile the array exactly as a grid: per split dimension the intervals cover the dimension end to end without overlap, every combination of intervals occurs exactly once, and every data variable is written by at least one task. The order of the entries inside a region does not matter. Irregular tilings that are not grids are rejected even if they do not overlap, since the planner never produces them.

The tiling check is linear in the number of tasks; a manifest for ten years of hourly data in daily tasks (3650 tasks, 4 variables, 10 levels) parses and validates in well under a second.

Strings must be strings and integers must be integers: "72" is not accepted for 72, true is not accepted as 1, and "time" is not accepted where a list of dimensions is expected. Lists are converted to tuples, so a hand-built WriteTask(..., variables=["tas"]) compares equal to one built with ("tas",).

Violations raise ManifestError with the location of the problem, for example:

ManifestError: tasks[3]: missing field 'levels'
ManifestError: task 'task-000004': region start 3 is not a multiple of the write unit 24 of 'tas' on level 9 along 'time'
ManifestError: manifest: 'pr' on level 7: task intervals along 'time' overlap at index 48; ...

schema_version remains the compatibility contract. It is checked first, so a manifest from an incompatible grid-doctor fails with "re-initialise the store" rather than with a missing field.

items.title: How tasks are planned
items.text: Parallel writes are only safe if no two writers ever touch the same zarr chunk. Zarr writes a chunk by reading it, modifying the part that changed and writing it back; two writers doing that at the same time lose one of the updates, silently. The planner therefore cuts regions only at chunk boundaries.

items.title: split: the task size
items.text:
split={"time": 72} asks for tasks of 72 time steps. The size is rounded up to a multiple of the least common multiple of the write units of all arrays along that dimension, on all levels:

Arrays along time Requested Effective Why all chunked by 24 72 72 already a multiple of 24 all chunked by 24 50 72 next multiple of 24 tas by 2, pr by 3 4 6 lcm(2, 3) = 6 sharded, shard 48, chunk 24 24 48 shards are the write unit

Rounding is logged at INFO level, and the effective sizes end up in manifest.split. The last region along a dimension may be shorter (744 = 10 × 72 + 24, so the eleventh time task covers 24 steps).

Several split dimensions give the cartesian product of their regions: split={"time": 72, "plev": 4} on 744 time steps and 12 pressure levels gives 11 × 3 = 33 regions.

Splitting along cell is not supported

Every pyramid level is derived from the finest one by aggregating four children per parent. A cell region of the finest level becomes a 4ᵏ times smaller region on a level k steps coarser, which is generally no longer chunk-aligned. init_pyramid_store rejects split={"cell": ...} with a ManifestError. Split along time, ensemble member, vertical level or any other non-spatial dimension.

items.title: Which variables go into a task
items.text:
Variables are grouped by the split dimensions they have (and the levels they appear on):

  • All variables with the same split dimensions share a task, so a worker reads and regrids the source region once for all of them. variables_per_task=1 gives one task per variable instead, which lowers the memory per worker at the price of reading the source several times.
  • Variables without any split dimension (a static land-sea mask, a 0-d scale factor) get their own task with an empty region. They are written exactly once. Small static fields can instead be written by the init itself with materialise=["sftlf"]; they then appear in the level's coords and in no task.
  • split=None (the default) plans a single task per variable group that covers the whole store. This is the degenerate case and mostly useful for testing.

items.title: What the init does not compute
items.text: Only coordinates and materialise variables are computed at init time. For lazy data variables the init writes metadata only, so it takes seconds even for stores with hundreds of thousands of chunks. The pyramid passed to the init therefore only needs the correct shapes, dtypes, chunks, encodings and attributes; you can build it lazily from the full source without fear.

items.title: When the target already exists
items.text:
A second init on the same path is the one thing that can destroy work: it re-creates every level store. init_pyramid_store therefore checks the target first and lets you choose with if_exists:

if_exists Target is empty Target has a pyramid with a manifest Target has stores but no manifest (killed init, save_pyramid output) "error" (default) initialise StoreExistsError StoreExistsError "resume" initialise return the stored manifest if the plan matches, else StoreExistsError StoreExistsError "overwrite" initialise re-initialise, new manifest_id re-initialise

Resume plans the tasks again from the pyramid you pass and the chunking of the stores that already exist, and compares the result with the stored manifest: path, zarr format, levels, array names, dims, shapes, chunks and dtypes, materialise, the effective split and every task's variables, region and levels. It also compares the coordinate values the init wrote (time, vertical levels, members, ...), so a pyramid of another time range with the same length is refused rather than resumed under the old labels. If everything matches it returns the stored manifest unchanged, with its manifest_id, and writes nothing. Tasks that already finished keep their markers. If anything differs, it raises and lists the differences:

StoreExistsError: cannot resume /scratch/project/era5: the stored
manifest d28efd88… was planned differently (split {'time': 72} !=
{'time': 48}). Use if_exists='overwrite' to discard it and start over.

StoreExistsError: cannot resume /scratch/project/era5: the stored
manifest d28efd88… was planned differently (level 9: coordinate 'time'
differs at time=0: pyramid has 2021-01-01T00:00:00, store has
2020-01-01T00:00:00). Use if_exists='overwrite' ...

What resume cannot see is a change in the data under unchanged labels (the same time steps re-processed with a fixed input file, say). In that case overwrite.

That makes re-submitting a conversion after a time-out safe and cheap: same parameters resume where the last run stopped, different parameters fail loudly instead of wiping the store. Two accidental submissions with the same parameters running at the same time are harmless as well, since they write identical data into identical, chunk-aligned regions.

A moved or copied store cannot be resumed (its manifest records the old path, which is where workers would write). Use "overwrite" there.

Overwrite discards the store and starts a new manifest. Use it only when nothing else is writing into the path.

One conversion per path at a time

grid-doctor does not lock a store. It assumes that only one conversion writes into a path at any time, and it cannot enforce that on a shared file system or object store.

What grid-doctor does guard against:

  • a second init on an existing path is refused unless you pass if_exists ("error" is the default),
  • "resume" only continues a store that was planned the same way and has the same coordinate values,
  • workers refuse tasks of an older manifest, edited tasks, and pyramids whose coordinates differ from the stored ones.

What it cannot prevent: an "overwrite" while workers of the previous run are still writing. A worker that already passed its checks keeps writing, into the new stores. It notices afterwards and fails with StaleTaskError ("re-initialised while task-… was writing"), but by then its data may sit in regions the new run has already marked as done, and check_pyramid_store of the new run can still report the store as complete.

So, before overwriting:

  1. make sure the previous run into that path has finished or is cancelled (status / cancel in reflow, or the scheduler);
  2. if you ever see the "re-initialised while … was writing" error, overwrite once more, with nothing else running.

When several people or runs convert at the same time, give each conversion its own path, or let the workflow tool allow only one active run per target.

The _grid_doctor/ directory is not part of any zarr store and does not disturb readers. Once a store is complete and published you may delete it; you only lose the ability to run check_pyramid_store against it.

items.title: Writing a task
items.text: gd.write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task, s3_options=None)

items.title: Full or pre-subset pyramid
items.text:
The pyramid a worker passes can have either shape along the split dimensions:

  • Full extent: the same lazy pyramid as at init time. The task region is selected inside write_pyramid_task. Simple, but every worker builds the full dask graph.
  • Only the task region (recommended): subset the source first and build the pyramid from that. Each worker opens, reads and regrids only its slice.
source = xr.open_mfdataset(files, chunks={"time": 24})
pyramid = source.isel(task.isel()).gd.create_healpix_pyramid(max_level=9)
gd.write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task)

For every split dimension, the length must be either the full length recorded in the manifest or exactly the region length; anything else is a ManifestError. The pyramid may contain extra variables or levels; they are ignored.

items.title: What is validated before anything is written
items.text:
1. The stored manifest has the task's manifest_id. If the store was re-initialised since the task was planned, a StaleTaskError is raised and nothing is written.
  2. The task is identical to the task with the same id in the stored manifest. The manifest guarantees that its tasks are chunk-aligned and disjoint; an edited or hand-built task has no such guarantee and is refused with a ManifestError.
  3. Every level and variable of the task exists in the pyramid.
  4. Dimension names match the store (dimension order may differ; the data is transposed).
  5. Non-split dimensions have exactly the stored length.
  6. The coordinate values in the task region match the ones the init stored. Workers never write coordinates, so a pyramid built from another time range of the same length would otherwise put its data under the stored labels. Values are encoded the way they are stored (units, dtype, packing) and compared exactly; arrays along cell (cell, latitude, longitude) are skipped, since they follow from the HEALPix index.

After the data is stored and before the completion marker is written, the worker reads the manifest id once more. If the store was re-initialised in the meantime, it raises StaleTaskError and writes no marker (see overwrite).

items.title: Chunk alignment inside a task
items.text: da.store writes every dask block independently. If a worker's dask chunks do not line up with the store's chunks (for example the init pyramid was chunked time=24 and the worker opened the source with time=10), two blocks would share a zarr chunk and race. The worker detects this, logs a warning starting with Rechunking ... and rechunks to the store's write units. Correctness is preserved, but rechunking costs memory and time, so open the source with the same chunks in both steps if you see the warning.

items.title: Retries and idempotency
items.text:
A task writes the same values into the same region every time it runs. Running a task twice, or running a task whose first attempt crashed halfway, is harmless. The completion marker is written only after all data of the task has been stored, so a crashed task never looks done.

A job killed by Slurm in the middle of a write (time limit, scancel) can leave a truncated chunk file on a POSIX file system; S3 uploads are atomic, so there it cannot. Because regions are chunk-aligned, the retry rewrites every chunk of its region completely, without reading the old content, which replaces the broken file (or deletes it, if the new chunk is all fill value). The marker itself is written atomically (temporary file plus rename, or a single upload), so it is either complete or absent.

items.title: Return value
items.text: write_pyramid_task returns the task itself. That sounds odd but is deliberate: in reflow, the output of the array job is then a WriteTask, which is_task_done can verify on a cache hit (see below).

items.title: S3
items.text:
Pass the credentials to every call with s3_options, exactly as for save_pyramid. Credentials are never written to the manifest, the tasks or the markers:

s3_options = gd.get_s3_options("https://s3.example.org", "~/.s3-credentials.json")
manifest = gd.init_pyramid_store(pyramid, "s3://bucket/era5", s3_options, split={"time": 72})
gd.write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task, s3_options)
gd.check_pyramid_store(manifest, s3_options)

items.title: Checking completeness
items.text:
report = gd.check_pyramid_store(manifest)          # or the path: "/scratch/project/era5"
report.complete           # True / False, also bool(report)
report.done_tasks         # ("task-000000", ...)
report.missing_tasks      # tasks without a valid marker
report.problems           # structural problems, see below
print(report.summary())
report.raise_if_incomplete()   # IncompleteStoreError with the summary

The check reads level metadata and lists the marker directory. It never reads data, so it is fast even for very large stores. A store is complete when all of the following hold:

  1. Same manifest. The stored manifest.json has the id being checked. If not, the store was re-initialised and this manifest's markers mean nothing.
  2. Same layout. Every level store opens, and every array and coordinate listed in the manifest exists with the recorded shape, write unit and dtype. Violations end up in report.problems.
  3. All tasks done. Every task has a marker with the right manifest_id. Markers of other manifests and unreadable markers are counted in report.stale_markers and otherwise ignored.

items.title: Why markers and not chunks?
items.text:
The obvious alternative, "every chunk of the region exists", does not work: zarr does not store chunks that contain only the fill value. For regional data (CORDEX on a global HEALPix grid), ocean-only variables over land, or any masked field, most chunks are legitimately absent, and there is no way to distinguish "never written" from "written, but all NaN". A marker written after the data is unambiguous.

If you still want to look at chunks, inspect_chunks=True lists the stored chunk keys and reports, per finished task, how many chunks of its region are absent in report.absent_chunks as (task_id, absent, expected). This is informational and never makes a store incomplete. A task of a global, gap-free field with absent chunks is suspicious; a task over the Sahara of an SST field with all chunks absent is not. The option lists every object of the inspected arrays, which can take a while on large S3 stores.

items.title: Retrying only what is missing
items.text:
report = gd.check_pyramid_store(manifest)
for task in manifest.select_tasks(report.missing_tasks):
    gd.write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task)

select_tasks returns the tasks in manifest order and raises KeyError for unknown ids.

items.title: Running it with reflow
items.text:
The three steps map onto three reflow jobs. The init returns list(manifest.tasks), which reflow fans out into one array element per task; the write array job hands its tasks to a final check job, which fails the workflow if anything is missing.

"""convert_era5.py: ERA5 to HEALPix with one array element per task."""

from typing import Annotated

import xarray as xr
from reflow import Param, Result, Workflow

import grid_doctor as gd

wf = Workflow("era5-healpix")


def build_pyramid(
    source: str, max_level: int, region: dict[str, slice] | None = None
) -> dict[int, xr.Dataset]:
    """Same pyramid in every job; workers pass their task region."""
    ds = xr.open_mfdataset(source, chunks={"time": 24}, parallel=True)
    if region:
        ds = ds.isel(region)
    return ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(max_level=max_level, method="conservative")


# Not cached: see "Caching" below.
@wf.job(cache=False, cpus=4, mem="16G", time="00:30:00")
def init(
    source: Annotated[str, Param(help="Glob of input files")],
    target: Annotated[str, Param(help="Pyramid root, local path or s3://")],
    max_level: Annotated[int, Param(help="Finest HEALPix level")] = 9,
    time_per_task: Annotated[int, Param(help="Time steps per array element")] = 72,
    overwrite: Annotated[bool, Param(help="Discard an existing store")] = False,
) -> list[gd.WriteTask]:
    manifest = gd.init_pyramid_store(
        build_pyramid(source, max_level),
        target,
        split={"time": time_per_task},
        # A re-submit continues an existing store; changed parameters fail.
        if_exists="overwrite" if overwrite else "resume",
    )
    return list(manifest.tasks)


@wf.job(
    array=True,
    array_parallelism=64,
    cpus=16,
    mem="64G",
    time="02:00:00",
    verify=gd.is_task_done,
)
def write(
    task: Annotated[gd.WriteTask, Result(step="init")],
    source: Annotated[str, Param(help="Glob of input files")],
    max_level: Annotated[int, Param(help="Finest HEALPix level")] = 9,
) -> gd.WriteTask:
    pyramid = build_pyramid(source, max_level, task.isel())
    return gd.write_pyramid_task(pyramid, task)


@wf.job(cpus=1, mem="4G", time="00:10:00")
def check(
    done: Annotated[list[gd.WriteTask], Result(step="write")],
    target: Annotated[str, Param(help="Pyramid root, local path or s3://")],
) -> gd.StoreReport:
    report = gd.check_pyramid_store(target)
    report.raise_if_incomplete()
    return report


if __name__ == "__main__":
    wf.cli()

Submit and follow it like any reflow workflow:

$ python convert_era5.py submit --run-dir /scratch/project/runs \
      --source 'era5/t2m/*.nc' \
      --target /scratch/project/era5_t2m --max-level 10 --time-per-task 168
$ python convert_era5.py status <run-id>
$ python convert_era5.py retry <run-id> --task write   # only the failed elements

Notes on the design:

  • Each WriteTask is self-contained. The array job does not need the manifest; reflow passes each element its own task. If a later job needs the full manifest, call gd.load_manifest(target) there, or return the manifest from a separate job and pass it with Result(step=..., broadcast=True).
  • Choose time_per_task by memory and wall-clock, not by node count. Each element regrids time_per_task steps of the source at max_level. Measure one element interactively first, then size the others. Many short elements also make retries cheaper.
  • array_parallelism caps how many elements run at once. Use it to protect the file system or an S3 endpoint from too many concurrent writers.
  • S3: read credentials inside each job (for example with get_s3_options) and pass them to all three calls. Do not pass secrets as reflow Params; those end up in the run database.

items.title: Caching
items.text:
reflow skips a job whose identity (name, version, inputs, upstream outputs) it has seen before. Two things to know:

  • The init job is declared with cache=False. In reflow 2604.4 the Param values of a job are not part of its cache identity. A cached init would therefore return the tasks of the previous target even if you change --target, and the array job would write into the old store. With cache=False, every submit runs the init again; with if_exists="resume" that is cheap and returns the stored manifest, so the tasks (and their manifest id) are the same as last time.
  • A re-submit only redoes what is missing. Because the tasks are identical, reflow finds the write elements that succeeded last time in its cache and skips them; only failed or timed-out elements run again. retry <run-id> --task write does the same within one run. To start over deliberately, submit with --overwrite, but only after the previous run into the same target has finished or been cancelled (see one conversion per path).
  • verify=gd.is_task_done on the array job. A write element is cached by its task, and every task carries the manifest id, so a re-initialised store never reuses old results. On a cache hit with verification enabled, is_task_done additionally confirms that the marker is still in the store (it was not deleted, the store was not re-initialised by someone else). For a manifest-returning job, is_current does the same for the manifest.

items.title: Local testing
items.text:
wf.run_local(run_dir=..., source=..., target=...) runs the whole workflow in one process, which is the quickest way to try a conversion on a small time range. With max_workers > 1, reflow runs array elements in a process pool. On Linux the default fork start method can deadlock once dask, numba or zarr threads exist in the parent; switch to spawn before running locally:

import multiprocessing
multiprocessing.set_start_method("spawn", force=True)
run = wf.run_local(run_dir="/tmp/run", max_workers=4, source=..., target=...)

On a cluster every array element is its own process, so this does not apply there.

items.title: Re-running and recovering
items.text: Situation What to do A few array elements failed (time limit, node failure) check_pyramid_store lists them in missing_tasks. In reflow: retry <run-id> --task write, or submit again with the same parameters. By hand: manifest.select_tasks(report.missing_tasks). Partially written regions are rewritten completely by the retry. The whole run was cancelled or the dispatcher died submit again with the same parameters. The init resumes the stored manifest and only missing tasks run. The init job hit its time limit There is no manifest, only init.json and partial stores; nothing else ran. Give the init more time and submit --overwrite. A task ran twice Nothing. Writes are idempotent. You want a different split or variables_per_task Run the init with if_exists="overwrite" (--overwrite). All written data is discarded and a new manifest is created. "resume" refuses and lists what changed. The source data changed Overwrite. Resume notices changed layouts (shapes, chunks, variables) and changed coordinate labels (another time range), not changed values under the same labels. Workers from an old run are still in the queue after a re-init Those that have not started fail with StaleTaskError without writing anything. Cancel them, and next time cancel the old run before overwriting: workers that were already writing may have written into the new stores (see one conversion per path). The store was deleted check_pyramid_store reports problems; is_current returns False. Run the init again. You want to publish the finished store Optionally delete <path>/_grid_doctor/. Readers never look at it.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Error or symptom Cause Fix ManifestError: no manifest at .../_grid_doctor/manifest.json The init has not finished, failed, or the path differs. Check the init job and the path. StaleTaskError: task-… belongs to manifest … The store was re-initialised after the task was planned. Use tasks from the new manifest. StaleTaskError: … re-initialised while task-… was writing An overwrite happened while this worker was writing. Overwrite again and let only one run write into the path. StoreExistsError: … already holds a pyramid if_exists="error" (the default) and the target is not empty. "resume" to continue, "overwrite" to start over. StoreExistsError: cannot resume …: … planned differently (…) The parameters or the source layout changed since the init. Restore the parameters, or overwrite. StoreExistsError: cannot resume …: there is no readable manifest (… has not finished …) The previous init was killed, or the path holds a store not written by init_pyramid_store. Overwrite. ManifestError: tasks[3]: missing field '…' or … must be … The manifest file (or a task passed through JSON) is truncated or was edited. Re-initialise, or fix the named field. ManifestError: … intervals along 'time' overlap / … gap along 'time' or … not a multiple of the write unit A manifest whose tasks no longer tile the arrays, typically after hand-editing. Re-initialise; never edit regions by hand. ManifestError: task-…: the pyramid does not match the coordinates stored by the init … The worker built its pyramid from other data than the init (another time range, other levels), or subset it differently from task.isel(). Build workers from the same source as the init, subset with task.isel(). ManifestError: task-… differs from the task stored in the manifest The worker received a task that is not the one the manifest planned. Pass the tasks from manifest.tasks unchanged. ManifestError: cannot split along 'cell' split contains a spatial dimension. Split along a non-spatial dimension. ManifestError: dimension 'time' has different lengths across variables/levels Levels or variables disagree on the split dimension. All levels of a pyramid must share it; check the source. ManifestError: … expected the full length N or the task region length M The worker built its pyramid from a different subset than the task region. Subset with source.isel(task.isel()), nothing else. ManifestError: … has dims … the store expects … Variable built differently in the worker than at init. Use the same build_pyramid in both steps. Warning Rechunking 'tas' to the store's write units Worker chunks differ from init chunks. Open the source with the same chunks in both steps. split[...]=N rounded up to M in the log N is not a multiple of the chunk size. Expected; pick a multiple to avoid surprises. Store complete but values all NaN in a region The source has no data there, or the pyramid was built from the wrong source. Compare report.absent_chunks with your expectations.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Fan-out writes need one store per level (structure="flat", the default). init_pyramid_store(..., structure="multiscales") writes the template of a single datatree store and returns None; tasks, split and if_exists="resume" are not supported for it yet.
  • Splitting is supported along non-spatial dimensions only.
  • All levels of the pyramid must share the length of every split dimension.
  • A variable that has no split dimension is written by a single task. For very large static fields at high levels that task is correspondingly large; materialise or a separate run are the options.
  • grid-doctor does not lock stores: only one conversion may write into a path at a time (see one conversion per path).
  • The manifest describes data variables only. Coordinates are written completely by the init; resume and workers compare their values (not those along cell), but changed data under unchanged labels is not detected.

See the Parallel writes API reference for all parameters.

items.title: Point data (satellite swaths, stations, trajectories)
items.text: This recipe converts point-sampled data to a HEALPix pyramid: anything where every sample carries its own latitude and longitude instead of sitting on a fixed grid. Typical sources are satellite Level-2 swath products (imager or radar granules), in-situ station records, and ship or aircraft trajectories.

items.title: Why not regrid_to_healpix?
items.text:
The ESMF weight path assumes a fixed source geometry:

  • No weight reuse. Every satellite granule has unique geometry, so the expensive weight-generation step could never be amortised.
  • Nearest smears globally. ESMF's nearest source-to-destination method assigns a value to every destination cell. With a global HEALPix target and a narrow swath as source, the whole sphere, antipodal ocean included, would receive swath values.

bin_to_healpix instead assigns each sample to the HEALPix cell containing it and reduces all samples per cell. In the oversampled limit (sample spacing much finer than the target cell spacing) the per-cell mean converges to the area-weighted mean, making it the binning analogue of conservative remapping; the per-cell mode is the analogue of nearest-neighbour for categorical fields.

Choose the level from the sample spacing

Pick the target level so that the HEALPix cell spacing (58.6° / 2**level) is coarser than the sample spacing, the same rule resolution_to_healpix_level applies to gridded data. A 1 km imager swath maps comfortably to level 12 (~1.6 km); binning it to level 14 (~0.4 km) would leave most cells empty and fabricate detail the samples cannot support.

items.title: Minimal example
items.text:
import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

# 1. Open: geolocation may be a data variable rather than a coordinate
ds = xr.open_dataset("granule.h5", group="ScienceData")

# 2. Bin to the finest level
finest = gd.bin_to_healpix(
    ds,
    level=11,
    agg={"radiance": "mean", "cloud_type": "mode"},
    lat_name="latitude",          # explicit names for non-standard products
    lon_name="longitude",
    fill_values={"cloud_type": 255},
    with_counts=True,             # coverage becomes auditable downstream
)

# 3. Coarsen: continuous variables by mean, categorical ones by mode
categorical = ["cloud_type"]
pyramid = {11: finest}
for level in range(10, -1, -1):
    pyramid[level] = xr.merge(
        [
            gd.coarsen_healpix(finest.drop_vars(categorical), level, coarsen_mode="mean"),
            gd.coarsen_healpix(finest[categorical], level, coarsen_mode="mode"),
        ],
        combine_attrs="override",
    )

# 4. Upload
gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    "s3://my-bucket/my-l2-product.zarr",
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options("https://s3.example.org", "~/.s3-credentials.json"),
)

Mixed continuous and categorical products are binned in one call: pass a mapping for agg. Each variable records its own grid_doctor_method (binned-mean or binned-mode). coarsen_healpix, however, chooses one mode for the whole dataset: with coarsen_mode="auto" it would average cloud_type as well. Coarsen the two groups separately, as above, and merge them. For a product with a single method, one coarsen_healpix call per level is enough.

items.title: Fill values
items.text:
Declared _FillValue and missing_value attributes are honoured automatically, and floating-point non-finite values are always treated as invalid. For products that do not declare their fills, pass them explicitly:

gd.bin_to_healpix(ds, 11, fill_values={"quality_flag": 0})

0 is accepted as a fill value: the check is is None, never truthiness. Do not rely on dtype conventions ("int16 means -32768"): products that break the convention will silently pass fill values into your means.

items.title: Accumulating many granules
items.text:
At level 12 the dense global array has about 200 million cells, while a single granule touches only a sliver of it. Bin each granule to the compact (sparse) form, which holds only the cells the granule covers:

# granule_paths: your list of files; open each like ds above
sparse_granules = [
    gd.bin_to_healpix(xr.open_dataset(path), level=12, agg="mean", dense=False, with_counts=True)
    for path in granule_paths
]

Where orbits overlap, merge the granules with count-weighted means, so that a cell seen by three orbits is not biased toward the last one written. The result equals binning all samples at once:

stacked = xr.concat(sparse_granules, dim="granule", join="outer")
counts = stacked["radiance_count"].fillna(0)
composite = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "radiance": (stacked["radiance"] * counts).sum("granule") / counts.sum("granule"),
        "radiance_count": counts.sum("granule"),
    },
    attrs=sparse_granules[0].attrs,
)

Expand to the dense representation once, right before coarsening and publishing, with sparse_to_dense.

items.title: Worked example: EarthCARE MSI
items.text:
EarthCARE MSI Level-2 frames are one concrete instance of this recipe: 2-D swath geolocation (along_track × across_track), ~500 m pixel spacing (level 13, ~0.8 km, at most; level 12 in practice), continuous radiances binned with mean and classification products (cloud mask, cloud type) binned with mode. Nothing in the workflow above is specific to EarthCARE: the same calls handle any L2 swath product.

Sphere and ellipsoid are different grids

Satellite geolocation is geodetic (WGS84). Binning assigns each position to the HEALPix cell that contains it, on the sphere by default or on the WGS84 ellipsoid with ellipsoid="WGS84" (or gd.config.ellipsoid). Both are equally accurate, but they are different grids: cells on the ellipsoid are shifted by up to ~0.13° (~14 km) relative to cells on the sphere, several to dozens of pixels at swath resolutions. Only compare data that uses the same definition; the output records which one it uses. See Sphere or ellipsoid in the technical decisions.

items.title: Regional grids (CORDEX)
items.text:
This recipe converts regional model output to a HEALPix pyramid, with CORDEX rotated-pole domains as the canonical case, and shows how to access the result. The output is a standard dense global store that is simply NaN outside the domain; with aligned chunks and NaN fill, storage and reads stay proportional to the domain, not the globe.

Nothing here needs special machinery. Rotated-pole grids are detected automatically (rlat/rlon come first among grid-doctor's dimension candidates, and the 2-D lat(rlat, rlon) coordinates classify the grid as curvilinear). Conservative remapping to a global HEALPix mesh leaves every cell without domain overlap unmapped, that is NaN.

items.title: Creation
items.text:
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

ds = xr.open_mfdataset("CORDEX/EUR-11/.../tas_*.nc")

# EUR-11: 0.11 deg -> level 9 (~0.115 deg cell spacing)
level = gd.resolution_to_healpix_level(gd.get_latlon_resolution(ds))

hpx = ds.gd.regrid_to_healpix(level, method="conservative")

items.title: Domain-edge cells: mask by coverage
items.text:
Conservative weights are normalised by the full destination-cell area, so a HEALPix cell only partly inside the domain receives weights summing to its coverage fraction. The default missing_policy="renormalize" then scales that partial sum back up to a full-cell value: a cell 5% inside EUR-11 gets a confident-looking value that represents 5% of its area, and the domain silently grows by up to one cell. "propagate" does not help here, because cells outside the domain are absent from the weight matrix rather than NaN sources, so edge cells come out biased low by the coverage factor instead.

The weight application has no coverage threshold yet, so mask by coverage explicitly. The coverage fraction is a field of ones remapped with the same conservative weights:

ones = xr.Dataset(
    {"coverage_fraction": xr.ones_like(ds["tas"].isel(time=0, drop=True))},
    coords=ds.coords,
)
coverage = ones.gd.regrid_to_healpix(level, method="conservative")[
    "coverage_fraction"
]

hpx = hpx.where(coverage >= 0.5)          # representativeness, cf. coarsening rule
hpx["coverage_fraction"] = coverage.fillna(0.0).astype("float32")

The 0.5 threshold is the same representativeness rule that min_valid_fraction applies during coarsening: a cell's value must cover at least half of its area. Publishing coverage_fraction makes the boundary auditable and lets strict users apply their own threshold; it is the gridded analogue of the <var>_count companions of binned point data. The weight file is reused, so remapping the ones costs almost nothing.

items.title: Categorical variables: the mask is mandatory
items.text:
For categorical fields, method="nearest" uses ESMF's nearest source-to-destination method, which assigns every global cell its nearest source value: a EUR-11 land-use field would paint European classes over the Pacific. The coverage mask from above is therefore not a refinement but a requirement:

landuse = ds_categorical.gd.regrid_to_healpix(level, method="nearest")
landuse = landuse.where(coverage >= 0.5)

items.title: Pyramid, storage, and upload
items.text:
Coarsen every level from the finest one and store the valid fractions, so that means over coarse levels can be weighted (see Access below):

pyramid = {level: hpx}
for lvl in range(level - 1, -1, -1):
    pyramid[lvl] = gd.coarsen_healpix(hpx, lvl, valid_fraction={"tas": True})

encoding = {
    lvl: {
        var: {"chunks": (4**6,), "_FillValue": np.nan}
        for var in pyramid[lvl].data_vars
    }
    for lvl in pyramid
}
gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    "s3://my-bucket/cordex-eur11-tas.zarr",
    encoding=encoding,
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options("https://s3.example.org", "~/.s3-credentials.json"),
)

Valid fractions are relative to the level they are coarsened from, which is why every level starts from hpx instead of the next finer level. Two encoding choices make the mostly-NaN globe cheap:

  • Power-of-four chunks. A chunk of length 4**k is exactly one level-(L-k) parent cell and therefore spatially compact, so only chunks whose parent intersects the domain contain data.
  • _FillValue = NaN. With NaN as the Zarr fill value, all-NaN chunks are not written at all (write_empty_chunks=False is the zarr-python default). Verified: a domain covering 3.0% of the sphere writes 3.1% of the chunks.

The 50% rule erodes the domain boundary by at most one parent cell per coarsening step. That is the representativeness policy working as documented, not data loss. Finally, add bounding-box attributes so that viewers can zoom to the domain instead of opening on an empty globe:

for lvl, dataset in pyramid.items():
    dataset.attrs.update(
        geospatial_lat_min=float(ds["lat"].min()),
        geospatial_lat_max=float(ds["lat"].max()),
        geospatial_lon_min=float(ds["lon"].min()),
        geospatial_lon_max=float(ds["lon"].max()),
    )

items.title: Access
items.text:
Regional stores at typical CORDEX levels (≤ 10) are ordinary HEALPix datasets: the coordinates are stored, viewers render them, and any HEALPix-aware tool works unchanged. NaN outside the domain is the expected state, not an error.

On the equal-area grid, a domain mean is just a NaN-aware mean, with no latitude weighting and no domain mask file:

import xarray as xr

ds9 = xr.open_zarr("s3://my-bucket/cordex-eur11-tas.zarr/level_9.zarr", chunks=None)
domain_mean = ds9["tas"].mean("cell", skipna=True)   # area-weighted by construction

This holds at the finest level of the pyramid, where every cell is either inside or outside the domain. On coarser levels, cells along the domain edge are only partly covered, and a plain mean gives them full weight. Weight by the stored valid fractions there, as shown in Coarsening and averaging masked fields:

ds5 = xr.open_zarr("s3://my-bucket/cordex-eur11-tas.zarr/level_5.zarr", chunks=None)
domain_mean = ds5["tas"].weighted(ds5["tas_valid_fraction"].fillna(0)).mean("cell")

Sub-domains are extracted with the same selectors as everything else, which read only the chunks the box touches:

import grid_doctor as gd

alps = ds9.gd.select_bbox(lon=(5.0, 16.0), lat=(43.0, 48.5))
alps["tas"].mean("cell", skipna=True)                # Alpine-box mean

And because nested cell IDs align across levels by construction, comparing the CORDEX domain against a global dataset needs no interpolation: select the same cells from both.

era5 = xr.open_zarr("s3://my-bucket/era5.zarr/level_9.zarr", chunks=None)
era5_alps = era5.gd.select_cells(alps["cell"].values)
bias = alps["tas"] - era5_alps["t2m"]                # cell by cell, exact

For evaluation workflows this is the payoff of one shared indexing geometry: differences between model and reanalysis are positional subtractions, never regridding.

items.title: Structured grids (ERA5, CMIP)
items.text: This recipe converts data on a regular or curvilinear lat/lon grid, such as ERA5 or CMIP6 output, to a HEALPix pyramid and writes it to S3.

items.title: Minimal example
items.text:
Open the data, get the weights for its grid and build the pyramid with conservative remapping, the default:

import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd

# 1. Open
ds = xr.open_mfdataset("era5_2m_temperature_*.nc")

# 2. Weights: computed once, then taken from the weights store
level = gd.resolution_to_healpix_level(gd.get_latlon_resolution(ds))
weights_file = gd.cached_weights(
    ds,
    level=level,
    store="/path/to/weights",
    nproc=4,
    prefer_offline=True,
)

# 3. Convert
pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(max_level=level, weights_path=weights_file)

# 4. Write
gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    "s3://my-bucket/era5/2t",
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options("https://s3.example.org", "~/.s3-credentials.json"),
)
  • level is the HEALPix level whose cell spacing matches the grid; pass another value to max_level (and level) to choose it yourself.
  • store is a local directory, possibly shared with others. Without it, the default store is used, see Weights store.
  • prefer_offline=True computes large conservative weights with the parallel ESMF_RegridWeightGen (with nproc MPI processes) instead of in memory.

items.title: Masked fields (ocean, sea ice)
items.text:
For variables with missing values, store the valid fraction of each cell so that averages over coarse levels stay consistent with the finest one (see Coarsening and averaging masked fields for how to use them):

pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(
    max_level=level,
    weights_path=weights_file,
    # land-sea masked SST: one cell-only fraction is enough;
    # sea ice changes over time and needs the full shape
    valid_fraction={"sst": "static", "siconc": True},
)

Variables without missing values do not need fractions.

items.title: Command-line script
items.text:
The same conversion as a script, using the parser from grid_doctor.cli:

import xarray as xr

import grid_doctor as gd
import grid_doctor.cli as gd_cli

parser = gd_cli.get_parser("era5", "Convert ERA5 to HEALPix.")
parser.add_argument("files", nargs="+")
parser.add_argument("--weights-store", help="Local directory of the weights store.")
args = parser.parse_args()
gd_cli.setup_logging_from_args(args)

ds = xr.open_mfdataset(args.files)
weights_file = gd.cached_weights(ds, store=args.weights_store, nproc=4, prefer_offline=True)
pyramid = ds.gd.create_healpix_pyramid(weights_path=weights_file)
gd.save_pyramid(
    pyramid,
    f"s3://{args.s3_bucket}/era5",
    s3_options=gd.get_s3_options(args.s3_endpoint, args.s3_credentials_file),
)

python convert.py --s3-bucket my-bucket --s3-endpoint https://s3.example.org \
    --weights-store /path/to/weights era5_*.nc -vv
